howToBuild.welcomeBody: Everything below is already running — the application, the accounts, the data. What is left is to connect a repository and start building. This welcome is shown once; the guide itself stays behind the button in the footer.
howToBuild.missing: The guide file is missing on the server. This is a deployment problem, not a wording one.
howToBuild.changeTitle: Changing the platform itself — tools, agents, your own solution
howToBuild.changeBody: Your project is yours: pages, logic, data, the whole application on port 3000. The platform underneath it — sign-in, the data layer, this panel, the services — is delivered ready and is replaced wholesale on every deployment, so a change made to it on this server would not survive the next one and is stored nowhere. Today there is exactly one way to get a change into the platform: ask the people who build it.
howToBuild.changeCopied: Copied — send it from your own email to admin@fractera.ai
howToBuild.changeMailHint: Send it from your own email to admin@fractera.ai. Nothing else is needed in this first letter: the address identifies your server, and we take it from there.

users.name: Name
users.unavailable: The authorization service did not answer, so the list could not be read. This is not the same as having no users.
users.rolesHint: Select one or more roles. You can't edit your own account — and only another architect can remove the architect role from someone.
users.blockBody: Block {email}? They will not be able to sign in.
users.unblockBody: Unblock {email}? They will be able to sign in again.
users.deleteBody: Permanently delete {email}? This cannot be undone.
users.helpLabel: Why this table has its own screen
users.helpWhat: Accounts, roles and access. Technically these are rows like any other, and you can read them in the database browser.
users.helpWhyTitle: Why it is not just a table.
users.helpWhy: This is the one table where a careless edit locks you out of your own server. Granting the architect role, or taking access away, should be one obvious action with a visible consequence — not an UPDATE typed into a grid next to forty other tables. The authorization service owns these rows and keeps sessions in step with them; editing them by hand can leave a session alive for an account that no longer has the right.
users.helpHow: Read users in the database browser when you want to understand. Change them here, where every action is named and confirmed.

media.empty: No files yet — upload your first media
media.unavailable: The data layer did not answer, so the library could not be read. This is not the same as having no files.

trimmer.title: Trim video — keep the middle
trimmer.lossless: The cut is lossless — the streams are copied, not re-encoded.
trimmer.tooShort: The kept part is too short

media.helpLabel: Object storage — files, compared with the database
media.helpHolds: The files themselves: images, video, audio, documents. Bytes, not rows. It streams them, serves them with cache headers, crops images and trims video.
media.helpVsDbTitle: How it differs from the database.
media.helpVsDb: The database holds facts about a file — its name, size, type, duration, who uploaded it and when. This holds the file. The split is not bureaucracy: files inside a database bloat it and make every backup slow, while facts kept only in a filesystem cannot be searched, filtered or joined. Each keeps what it is good at, and they point at each other.
media.helpCost: Disk, and nothing else. No model, no per-request billing — the storage lives on your server, so a file served a million times costs the same as one served once.
media.helpWeak: It knows nothing about content. A PDF is a sequence of bytes to it; until something extracts the text and puts it in vector memory or the knowledge base, nobody can ask a question about what is inside.

vector.unavailable: The data service did not answer, so the store could not be read.
vector.noKey: Without an OpenAI key text cannot be turned into vectors, and both writing and searching answer with an honest error. Paste one in
vector.askSomething: Ask the warehouse a question — the closest records answer here.
vector.helpLabel: Vector search — what it does differently
vector.helpGet: The passages closest in meaning to your question, each with a score. Not an answer — the raw material for one. Nothing is written for you.
vector.helpWhy: One phase. Text is split into chunks, each chunk becomes a vector, and a search compares your question's vector against them. Nothing is precomputed about how facts relate, so nothing has to be paid for in advance.
vector.helpWins: When the answer sits in one passage: prices, policies, product facts, “how do I connect X”. It is also the right home for data that keeps changing — a changed row costs one embedding call to re-index, while a graph would have to extract its relations again.
vector.helpCost: Almost nothing. Ingest is one embedding call per chunk; a search is milliseconds against a real index, and its cost does not grow with the size of the store.
vector.helpWeak: It knows no relations. A question that needs forty documents makes something read all forty. And it never composes an answer — you, or an agent, must do that. An agent looping over this store can beat the graph on flexibility, because it can rephrase and search again; it pays per question instead of paying once at ingest.
vector.helpSeparateTitle: The two do not share storage.
vector.helpSeparate: Vectors live in the data service's SQLite, in the vectors table beside your rows. The graph lives in the RAG service's own folder. To have a document in both, upload it to both: you pay each one's ingest and get each one's kind of answer. Nothing is shared but the OpenAI key.

rag.serviceOff: The service is stopped, so there is nothing to read or ask. Turning it off is a legitimate choice — it costs memory even while idle.
rag.noKey: This service needs the key in its OWN env, and its failure is silent: ingest answers 200 and embeds nothing. Save the key once in
rag.ingestTitle: Add a document to the graph
rag.ingestHint: Paste text. The service extracts entities and relations from it — that is what a graph gives over a passage search, and that is what it charges for at ingest.
rag.wipeBody: Every document, entity and relation is removed. The files uploaded to storage are not touched — this is only the graph.
rag.askPlaceholder: a question in your own words…
rag.askWarning: an answer takes tens of seconds
rag.emptyAnswer: The graph returned an empty answer — most often that means the base has nothing on the subject yet.
rag.noDocuments: The base is empty — add a document to have something to ask about.
rag.helpLabel: The knowledge graph — relations, compared with vector search
rag.helpGet: A composed answer, not a list of passages. The service reads across documents and writes the reply itself.
rag.helpWhy: Two phases. At ingest a model extracts entities and the relations between them into a graph; at question time that graph is walked. The thinking is paid for in advance, once per document, instead of at every question.
rag.helpWins: When the answer is spread across many documents and depends on how facts connect: who is related to whom, what follows from what, summaries over a whole corpus.
rag.helpCost: Noticeably more than vectors, and mostly at ingest: every document is read by a model. A question is cheap by comparison, but never free — it also goes through a model.
rag.helpWeak: Changing data. A corrected document has to be re-read from scratch, relations and all, while a vector store needs one embedding call. And the graph decides itself what mattered in your text — you cannot see the passage its answer came from as directly.
rag.helpSeparateTitle: The two do not share storage.
rag.helpSeparate: The graph lives in this service's own folder; vectors live in the data service's SQLite. To have a document in both, add it to both: you pay each one's ingest and get each one's kind of answer. Nothing is shared but the OpenAI key.

map.intro: Maps, routing and address search for your automations — self-hosted on free OpenStreetMap data, any region on Earth, no third-party keys.
map.loadError: Could not reach the geo service.
map.noRegionHint: The engines are installed, but no map region is loaded yet — and that is on purpose: the whole planet cannot fit on a server, so guessing a region for you would waste around 10 GB on a map you would replace anyway. Tell the assistant below where you actually work.
map.quizGreeting: Which places do you need maps for? Name the cities or areas — I'll ask if anything's unclear and pick the available regions.
map.noKey: The region assistant needs an OpenAI key. Save one in OpenAI settings.
map.checkLabel: Check the regions to download — size and time are shown honestly
map.noneFound: Nothing available was found. Try naming the country or a larger area.
map.provisioningNote: Loading runs in the background; bigger regions take longer. Several checked regions are merged into one. Address search comes online when it finishes.
map.helpLabel: Maps — your own routing engine, and what it is for
map.helpWhat: A map engine running on your server, built from OpenStreetMap data: routing and geocoding, behind one address your automations call. No third-party map key, no per-request billing, no quota that stops your business on a busy day.
map.helpAnswers: An address into coordinates. A route from A to B with its distance and driving time. A matrix of distances and times between many points at once. And the best order to visit a set of stops — the classic travelling-salesman solve.
map.helpWorthTitle: What that is worth in practice.
map.helpWorth: A courier with twelve deliveries: the matrix gives every pair of times, the tour solve gives the order that spends the least time driving. Fuel follows from the same numbers — total distance times your consumption — so “which route is cheapest today” stops being a guess. The same answers give an honest delivery window to a customer, tell you whether an address falls inside your service area, and let a dispatcher compare two plans before anyone leaves the depot.
map.helpWhyOwnTitle: Why it is here and not bought.
map.helpWhyOwn: Commercial map APIs charge per request, and routing is the kind of thing an automation does thousands of times. Self-hosting turns a growing bill into fixed disk and CPU that you already pay for.
map.helpCost: One region at a time. The engine holds an extract — a country or an area — and importing a new one takes minutes and disk. Choose the region you actually work in, not the largest one available.
map.helpWeak: It knows roads, not traffic: times come from speed limits and road classes, not from what is happening right now. Treat them as reliable planning numbers rather than live estimates.

addTool.body: The tools above are not the full list of what can run on your server. More can be added as part of the project — running on your machine, behind your own address, with no third-party key and no per-request bill:
addTool.exampleFlow: a flow and diagram builder (React Flow)
addTool.how: Write to us with what you need and what it is for. By agreement the developer connects to your server and sets the tool up in place — you get it as a native part of the project, not as another subscription.
addTool.mailSubject: New tool for my Fractera project
addTool.note: Say what the tool should do and where it fits in your work. That is enough for a first reply — a precise specification is not expected of you.

backup.secretWarning: The two parts marked “secret” contain credentials: with them, anyone who opens the archive can act as your bot or reach your services. They are unchecked by default. If you tick them, keep the file off shared drives and out of chats.
backup.neverExported: The OpenAI key is never exported — you enter it again after restoring. Map data is never exported either: it is over a gigabyte, and the map page re-downloads its region on demand.
backup.defaultTotal: ≈ {size} with the default selection, before compression
backup.nothingYet: Nothing is written until you choose what to restore. The archive is read first and its contents are listed here.
backup.unrecognised: Nothing recognisable inside. This does not look like a Fractera backup.

backup.helpExportLabel: What a backup is made of
backup.helpWhat: Your rows and the meaning-search over them travel together — they share one SQLite file. Files come with the record of what each one is. The knowledge graph is the most expensive part here: rebuilding it means paying for a model to read every document again.
backup.helpWhen: Before anything that rewrites data — a restore, a migration to another machine, a risky experiment. A deploy does not need one: it restores code, and code lives in your repository.
backup.helpNotTitle: What a backup does not cover.
backup.helpNot: It is code-blind. Restoring an archive does not bring back the version of your application that produced the data, and a build rolled back does not roll back rows. Those are two different histories, kept in two different places on purpose.
backup.helpAdds: Rows and files are merged: what you already have keeps its value, and only what is missing is written. Running an import twice changes nothing the second time.
backup.helpReplaces: The graph, application settings, channels and the environment file are written over what is here now. Those rows are marked in amber above, and the secret ones are left unchecked — a token or an environment must never be swapped by silent agreement.
backup.helpOrder: The archive is inspected on the server first and its contents are listed. Nothing is touched until you confirm the parts — this is the one page where a mistake is not undone by pressing the other button.

domain.unavailable: The domain status could not be read.
domain.entryIntro: Enter the domain you bought, in apex form (for example aifa.dev). The steps that follow walk through the DNS records, the certificate, an end-to-end HTTPS check, and the switch from IP mode to your domain.
domain.entryInvalid: Enter a valid domain (for example myapp.com)
domain.cloudflareWarning: Do not use Cloudflare DNS. Cloudflare proxies traffic through their network, which adds a dependency and occasional connectivity trouble. Use your registrar's own DNS panel — they all give you direct A-record management.
domain.entrySaved: Domain saved — continue with the steps below
domain.dnsIntro: Add all {n} A-records below at your DNS provider — your registrar's own panel, not Cloudflare. Each one points to the same address:

dnsNotes.ai-browser: AI browser for services and agents

domain.checkDns: I added the records — check DNS
domain.dnsAllOk: Every A-record resolves to this server
domain.dnsStillMissing: Still not resolving: {hosts}. DNS can take a few minutes to propagate.
domain.dnsNotPropagated: DNS is not fully propagated yet — give it a few minutes and check again.
domain.changeConfirm: Change the domain from {domain}?\n\nNothing is live yet — this only clears the saved domain so you can type the correct one. You will re-add the DNS records for the new domain.
domain.trustQuestion: Why do we not ask for your server password?
domain.trustBody: Issuing a certificate traditionally means logging into the server over SSH. Fractera never does that. The panel you are using runs as an application ON YOUR OWN SERVER and issues the certificate locally through certbot. Nothing connects in from outside, and your server password is never received or stored.
domain.trustProof: Proof you can verify yourself: change your server's root password right now. Issuance will still work exactly the same — because this panel is your own application on your own machine and has no way to reach into your server.
domain.autoLabel: Use an automatic Let's Encrypt certificate (free, recommended)
domain.autoHint: Uncheck only if you must install your own certificate — a regulated region, or an EV/OV certificate from a specific authority.
domain.autoNote: One certbot call issues a single certificate covering every hostname. Renewal runs by itself roughly every 60 days through the system certbot timer.
domain.issueStarted: Issuance started — this takes 60 to 120 seconds
domain.issueDone: Certificate issued — it covers every hostname
domain.issueFailed: Issuance failed — the reason is shown in this step
domain.issueSlow: Still working… use “Refresh status” to see the result.
domain.lastFailedHint: Usually one hostname is not resolving yet — check the list above, then press “Issue certificate” again.
domain.uploadHint: Paste a PEM chain and a private key. It must cover every hostname, or include a wildcard *.{domain} alongside the apex. Certificates from any authority are accepted.
domain.bothRequired: Both the certificate and the key are required
domain.healthIntro: The final check: for every hostname we resolve DNS and open an HTTPS connection with strict certificate validation. A failure here means switching to secure mode would break that address.
domain.healthAllOk: Every hostname answers over HTTPS with a valid certificate
domain.healthOkOptional: Required hostnames are fine — you can activate. Not responding yet: {hosts} (does not block activation).
domain.healthFailing: A required hostname is still failing — details below
activateBullets: every admin address moves from http://<ip>:port to https://{domain}
this tab is redirected to https://admin.{domain}
the demo session ends — the first user to register becomes the administrator
a message with the new addresses goes to your account email
if anything breaks within 30 seconds, the server reverts to IP mode by itself and you stay on this panel
domain.activateConfirm: Activate secure mode on {domain}? You will be redirected to https://admin.{domain} and will need to sign in.
domain.activateStarted: Switching to secure mode — this takes a few seconds, and you will be redirected automatically. Check your email for the new addresses.
domain.liveIntro: {domain} is live, secured by a {cert} certificate.
domain.renewNote: Renews by itself roughly every 60 days through the system certbot timer.
domain.reissueSoon: Manual renewal ships in a future update
domain.emailIntro: Email yourself the full list of your new HTTPS addresses — a useful reminder later. Future server and certificate notices arrive at the same address.
domain.emailSent: Email sent to {recipient}. Check the spam folder — if you find it there, move it to the inbox and mark it “not spam” so later notices arrive reliably.
domain.rollbackIntro: Need to roll back? You can return to plain-HTTP IP mode at any time — your domain and certificate stay configured for re-activation.
domain.rollbackConfirm: Switch back to IP mode?\n\n{domain} stays configured, but the project is served over plain HTTP on its IP again and the demo session returns. You can re-activate secure mode at any time.
domain.switchingBack: Switching back — redirecting in a few seconds…
domain.footnote: This is the only page that changes how the whole server is reached. Nothing here happens without your press.
domain.helpLabel: What attaching a domain actually does
domain.helpWhat: Your project stops being an IP address with ports and becomes a set of addresses on your own domain, each over HTTPS: the site, sign-in, this panel, the data layer. The certificate is issued on your server, so no traffic passes through anybody else.
domain.helpDns: Each service answers on its own hostname, and every hostname needs its own A-record pointing at the same server. One certificate then covers them all at once, which is why a single missing record blocks issuance for everything.
domain.helpSafety: Nothing switches until the end-to-end check passes on every required hostname. And if something breaks within 30 seconds of activation, the server returns to IP mode by itself — you keep this panel rather than losing your way in.
domain.helpBack: Switching back to IP mode is one button and keeps the domain and certificate configured. That is deliberate: a change to how a server is reached must never be a one-way door.

channels.serviceDown: The channels service is not running, so nothing can be set up here yet.
channels.tokenRejected: The token is saved, but Telegram does not recognise it. Either it was mistyped, or it was revoked in @BotFather — get a fresh one there and save it again.
channels.tokenReplace: Paste a new token to replace the saved one
channels.linkTimeout: Linking timed out — press Connect again.
channels.linkExpired: The code expired — press Connect again.
channels.answersFrom: Once linked, the bot answers from the knowledge base built in
channels.neverInvents: It never invents an answer: with the base empty or the service off, it says so.
channels.helpLabel: What a channel is, and what it is not
channels.helpWhat: A door into your project from a messenger instead of a browser. A person writes to your bot and gets an answer built from your own knowledge base — no separate app, no login screen.
channels.helpWhyTitle: Why your own bot and not ours.
channels.helpWhy: The token belongs to a bot you created, so the conversation runs between your visitors and your server. Nothing passes through us, and if you ever move the server the bot moves with the token.
channels.helpLinkTitle: Why linking needs a one-time code.
channels.helpLink: The link is opened inside a messenger, where it is visible to anyone who sees the screen. A code that worked twice would let someone else attach their account to your project, so it works once and expires.
channels.helpOff: The switch stops the bot answering without deleting the token or the link — useful while you are changing the knowledge base and would rather nobody got half-built answers.
channels.scheduleHint: How often the product is asked whether a reminder has come due. Reminders have to fire while nobody is looking at the site, so something has to knock — this is it. Off means the project has no reminders and pays for none.
channels.introIntro: This is what the bot answers on /start and on «what can you do». It is not a setting: it describes what the product really does today, so it changes with the product, not from this page.
introAbilities: listen by voice or text — a voice note is transcribed and treated exactly like typing
remember WHEN it happened, not only when it was told: «yesterday I bought…» is stored under yesterday
understand what it was told — a purchase, a task, a place, a promise — and keep the useful fields, such as an amount and a vendor
mark anything involving money, so «what did I spend» is answered from a column instead of re-reading a year
keep the location when one is sent
search by MEANING, not by words: «where did I buy electronics» finds the shop even when that word appears nowhere
build a knowledge graph out of everything, so connections between separate days can be found later
set reminders and events, one-off or repeating, warning in advance when asked — and it always reads the time back before setting it
introCommands: «запомни …» — remember as a promise, not as a passing note
«напомни … в …» — a reminder at a time; it names the time and asks first
«напоминай каждый рабочий день в 9 …» — repeating: daily, weekdays, weekly, monthly
«запланируй встречу … в 10, напомни за час» — an event with advance warning
«найди …», «когда я …», «сколько я …» — search their own history
channels.introNotYet: Storing files. A photo, a video or a PDF arrives with its caption saved, but the file itself is not yet kept in the media library. Until it is, the assistant deliberately does not offer it — a promise nobody keeps is discovered at the worst moment, when someone relied on it.

openai.intro: One key, entered once, that every thinking part of the platform draws on. It is not a plan with a monthly fee — it is a balance you top up, charged for what was actually used. A balance from $5 is enough to start; get a key at
openai.replace: Paste a new key to replace the saved one
openai.saved: Key saved — the services restart to pick it up
openai.invalid: That does not look like an OpenAI key (expected sk-…)
openai.mismatch: The key reached one consumer but not another. This is the failure worth catching: the knowledge graph fails SILENTLY — it accepts a document with a success answer and embeds nothing, and the application answers "no key" to voice input. Save the key again; it is written to all three.
openai.storedLocally: The key is stored only on your own server, in the services' own environment files. It is never sent anywhere else and never shown back to this page — what you see is a state, not the value.
openai.helpLabel: One key — what spends it, and why this is not a subscription
openai.helpWhat: One key that every part of the platform draws on. You are charged for what was actually used, down to the request, instead of paying a flat fee for capacity you may not touch.
openai.helpSpends: Vector memory turns each chunk of text into a vector — once at ingest, once per search. The knowledge graph spends far more: it reads every chunk to extract entities and relations, then writes an answer for each question. Voice input pays for transcription by the minute; images pay a vision model by the picture. Different jobs, different models, different prices — a search costs a fraction of a cent, a graph pass over a long document costs minutes of compute.
openai.helpNoSubTitle: Why a subscription cannot replace it.
openai.helpNoSub: No single flat plan covers this shape of work: embeddings, transcription, vision and reasoning are separate services priced separately. More to the point, most consumer plans restrict commercial use and many forbid automated or agent-driven access outright — which is exactly what a platform like this does all day. A pay-as-you-go key is not a workaround; it is the only arrangement that is both permitted and predictable.
openai.helpSavingTitle: What we do about the cost.
openai.helpSaving: Tokens are treated as money, because they are. Embeddings run on the cheap text-embedding-3-small rather than the large model — the quality difference is imperceptible for this work and the price is about seven times lower. The vector store answers from a real index, so a search reads a handful of rows instead of the whole base. The graph pays its expensive pass once at ingest and stays cheap per question afterwards.
openai.helpWatch: Loading a large corpus into the knowledge base is the one operation that costs real money in a single go. Load what you will actually ask about, and remember that re-loading a document pays for that pass again.
openai.helpProvider: OpenAI is the default chosen for the balance of price, quality and availability. If your project needs a different provider or model, write to
openai.whyTitle: Why the project is built with Claude models while the key here is OpenAI
openai.whyDev: These are two different things, and they do not contradict each other. Your project's code is written by a developer on their own machine, in Claude Code, with Claude models — Sonnet, Opus, Fable. The key on this page is not for development: it powers the services that run ON YOUR SERVER and answer your visitors — the Quiz, vector search, the knowledge graph.
openai.whyEmbeddings: The decisive reason is technical, not a matter of taste. Vector search and the knowledge graph rest on text embeddings. Anthropic does not make them: its documentation states verbatim, «Anthropic does not offer its own embedding model», and points to a third-party provider. A product that needs search by meaning must take embeddings where they exist.
openai.whyBudget: The second reason is about money, and it is about keeping two budgets apart. A Claude subscription is issued to a PERSON: it is an allowance for their own work, shared with chat and running on rolling windows. A server answering visitors is a different kind of load — continuous, and growing with traffic. That belongs on a metered API key, not on a developer's working allowance: otherwise the first surge of visitors eats the very thing the project is built with.
openai.whySwap: The key is yours, the cost goes straight to your provider, and we never see it. The list of providers is not carved in stone: the moment the services we use gain another suitable option, it will appear here too.
openai.whyDocTitle: Why the key here is OpenAI: three budgets and one trap

deployments.unavailable: The history could not be read — the data layer did not answer.
deployments.copied: Log copied — paste it to your coding agent
deployments.copyFailed: The browser refused to copy — select the log and copy it by hand, or download it.
deployments.autoHint: The server asks the repository once a minute and acts only after it has been still for two minutes, so a burst of pushes becomes one build. Nothing is configured on GitHub for this.
deployments.helpLabel: Why the history lives in the database
deployments.helpWhyTitle: A failed build stops being a moment.
deployments.helpWhy: Every press of Deploy is recorded in your project's database, not in a file the next restart forgets. The log is still there tomorrow, after a reload, after a restart of the panel — you do not have to reproduce a failure to read its cause again. And because it lives in the same storage as the rest of your data, an agent can query “what happened on the last five deploys” instead of investigating.
deployments.helpModes: Manual — nothing happens without your button. Pull only — the server fast-forwards to the repository; content and pages apply at once, code waits for your Deploy. Pull and deploy — the server pulls and builds, the way a hosting platform does. The difference matters because this server builds on the same machine that serves your visitors: a build competes with the site for the processor.
deployments.helpRefuses: If this server holds uncommitted changes, if the histories have diverged, or if a build is already running, the turn is skipped and the reason appears above. Only a clean fast-forward is taken automatically — your work is never buried to make room.
deployments.helpOffTitle: Why it is off by default.
deployments.helpOff: On a project serving real customers, letting a build start by itself is a decision to make deliberately rather than inherit. So the default is Manual, and turning it on is one press with the cost stated.
deployments.pickRun: Pick a deployment on the left to read its log.

github.unavailable: The connection status could not be read.
github.unverifiedHint: The details are saved but GitHub has not confirmed them. Usually the token lacks the repo scope, or the address points at a repository it cannot reach. Press Connect again to have GitHub check.
github.notConnected: Until this is connected, nothing you build here can leave the server. The data export carries your rows, files and knowledge — but not your source code. Git is the only road out for that.
github.step1Body: Open your repository on GitHub and copy the address from the browser bar, or from the green Code button. It looks like https://github.com/owner/name.
step2Steps: The link above lands on “Tokens (classic)”. Press “Generate new token” and choose “Generate new token (classic)”.
“Note” — a name for yourself, so you recognise it in a year. Something like “Fractera server”. GitHub does not use it.

“Expiration” — pick a date. When it passes, pushing simply stops working and you come back here with a new token. A long expiry is convenient, a short one is safer; “No expiration” works but means a leaked token stays useful forever.

“Select scopes” — the long list. Tick exactly ONE: “repo”, the first line, described as “Full control of private repositories”. Its five indented children tick themselves — that is expected. Touch nothing else: packages, workflows, org and admin scopes are not needed here, and every extra tick widens what a stolen token could do.
Scroll to the bottom and press “Generate token”.
Copy it at once. GitHub shows the value one time only; leave the page and it cannot be read again — only replaced.
Paste it into the token field below and press “Connect and verify”. If GitHub refuses it, the reason appears here rather than later during a push.
github.step2Note: A public repository can be read without a token, but writing to any repository needs one.
github.step2Saved: A token is already saved — leave the field empty to keep it.
github.step3Body: Connecting asks GitHub straight away whether these credentials actually reach that repository. Green above means a real answer came back — not that the fields are filled in.
github.step4Body: Connecting the credentials does not move a single file. Sending does: it packages what is on the server right now and puts it in your repository. Until it runs, the repository stays empty — which reads as “it did not work”.
github.step4Check: How to tell it worked: open the repository in a browser and refresh. Files appear, and the commit list shows one entry from this server. If the page is still empty, the answer from git below says why.
github.tokenReplace: Paste a new token to replace the saved one
github.helpLabel: What connecting a repository is for
github.helpWhyTitle: Why it is needed at all.
github.helpWhy: Nothing built here can leave this server without it. The repository is how your project travels to your own machine, to a teammate, and back — and how it survives the server itself.
github.helpFirstTitle: The first transfer goes the other way.
github.helpFirst: Your project already exists on this server, so the first push is from the server TO GitHub — it fills your empty repository with the starting point. After that the direction reverses for good: you push from your machine, the server pulls.
github.helpToken: A classic token with the repo scope, and a long lifetime: when a token expires, pushing simply stops working with no other warning. The token is stored on your server only, and pressing Connect does not merely save it — GitHub is asked whether it actually works.
github.helpData: Pages, components and configuration travel through git. Rows, uploaded files and vectors stay on the server and are not in the repository at all — they are backed up separately, in Export data. Restoring a repository does not bring data back, and restoring data does not bring code back.

launch.chooseTitle: How do you want to start?
launch.chooseLead: Two roads lead into development, and they are not interchangeable. Pick one — the rest of this page appears after you do.
launch.starterBody: This server already carries a working starter project. You create an empty repository on GitHub, send the starter into it, and develop from there.
launch.starterCta: Put the Fractera starter on GitHub
launch.starterMore: Nothing is downloaded and nothing is replaced: the project you already have becomes yours on GitHub. This is also the road to take if you plan to move an existing project onto Fractera later — that migration starts from a working starter.
launch.adoptBody: You already have a project built on the Fractera architecture and kept on GitHub. This server drops its own starter and runs your project instead.
launch.adoptCta: Connect a repository with a Fractera project
launch.adoptMore: The starter now on this server is destroyed, and nothing brings it back except installing it again. Your settings, your data and your uploaded files stay where they are. Connect a repository that really is built on the Fractera architecture: a project from another framework will not build, and the panel will say so rather than guess.
launch.machineOnly: This step closes with a check, not with a tick: the answer comes from GitHub.
launch.restartBody: The wizard returns to the choice screen and every tick you set is cleared. Claude Code on your machine is not touched — a mark about a program you installed is not ours to erase.
launch.restartKeep: Start over, keep the GitHub connection
launch.restartWithGithub: Start over and erase the GitHub connection
launch.restartWithGithubHint: The repository address and the access key are deleted from this server. You will have to enter them again.

launch.firstPromptText:
We are starting development of a Fractera project.

Project repository: {repoUrl}

IMPORTANT, ORDER OF WORK: in the next step I will hand you the environment file .env.local.
The project will not start without it. DO NOT install dependencies and do not run a build
until that file is with you — wait for it.

For now: read the project instruction and tell me you understand the setup and are waiting
for the environment.
launch.firstChangeText:
We are starting development, and I want you to begin with STEP NUMBER ONE.

Always follow the development-steps instruction: open a new step, create the current-steps
document, and close the step with a result when you finish. This is a project rule and it
applies from the very first change, even while the folder is still empty.

This is our first test step — short, a warm-up really.

Task: ask me what my company is called. When you have the answer, put that name into the
page title THROUGH THE CONFIGURATION FILE, not by editing markup.

Record the step in all three documents as the instruction requires. When you are done, tell
me that my company name is now visible on every page of the project, and make a commit so I
can see the change in the browser.
launch.firstDeployText:
Next development step: the first deployment of the project to a real server.

Use your own understanding of this project architecture to carry out the deployment. Run
the work as a development step, as usual.

A first deployment usually takes longer than the rest: you have to work out how this
application is put together. Errors may appear during it — that is normal.

IMPORTANT: so that we never repeat them, we keep a document called ANTI-PATTERNS. Its job
is to hold the knowledge of what should not have been done. Write everything you learn on
this deployment as the FIRST entry in that document: symptom, mechanism, cure.

When you are done, tell me the address where I will see the changes on the internet.
launch.finishTitle: You have mastered working with a programming agent
launch.finishLead: From here you develop the project yourself. Everything below is worth knowing before you start.
launch.finishAskTitle: Ask the agent — it knows this project
launch.finishAskBody: The agent holds the full picture of this architecture and how it works. If something is unclear, keep asking until it has explained the whole process to you. There is no such thing as too many questions here.
launch.finishStepsTitle: Every task begins with one phrase
launch.finishStepsBody: The whole project is built on development steps. Saying this lets the agent set aside resources, open a branch correctly and tie the work to the steps already finished. It is one of the things that will save you real money on every run.
launch.finishStepsPhrase: Create a new development step in which we will…
launch.finishBye: We wish you a happy journey with a professional tool for generating applications and automation.
launch.finishContact: Questions, or something not working? Write to us:
launch.adoptUrlLabel: Repository address of your Fractera project
launch.adoptConfirmTitle: The starter template will be destroyed permanently
launch.adoptConfirmBody: Everything currently standing in the slot will be removed and replaced with the contents of that repository. The control panel is unaffected — it runs on its own port. Nothing is touched until the repository has answered.

I would like to move my existing project to the Fractera architecture.

Repository: {repoUrl}

Please tell me what is needed from my side.

githubAbout.confirmHint: Fetching overwrites what is on this server with what is in the repository.
githubAbout.okHint: Open the deployments page to watch it.
githubAbout.failHint: Check the repository address and the access token on the connection page.
githubAbout.intro: Three buttons move your project between three places: this server, your repository on GitHub, and the live application your visitors see. Here is what each one does and in which direction.
githubAbout.pushTitle: Push — from this server to GitHub
githubAbout.pushBody: Sends what exists here to the repository. Used once at the start, to fill an empty repository with the starting point, and afterwards only when work was done in the panel itself.
githubAbout.pullTitle: Pull — from GitHub to this server
githubAbout.pullBody: Brings in what you pushed from your own machine. Content and pages apply at once; code still needs a deploy to become the running application.
githubAbout.deployTitle: Deploy — from files to the running application
githubAbout.deployBody: Compiles the application and restarts it. It does not touch the repository at all: it turns the files that are already here into what your visitors see.
githubAbout.filesVsDataTitle: Files travel through git — data never does.
githubAbout.filesVsData: Rows, uploaded files and vectors live on the server and are shared with your local copy while you develop. They are not in the repository, so a clone does not carry them and a push does not send them. The trap is that settings changed in this panel are FILES: your local copy will not know about them until you pull.
githubAbout.rule: use one place at a time. Start every session with Pull, finish every session with Push. Working in the panel and on your machine at the same time is the one common way to create a conflict here.
githubAbout.conflict: you will be told in plain terms. Take the message to your machine, resolve it there with your agent's help, then push and pull as usual.

env.warning: This is the raw environment of your project. A wrong value here does not fail loudly — it changes how a service behaves, or stops it starting. Prefer the dedicated pages (App settings, Languages, Login methods, OpenAI) where a value is validated before it is written.
env.unavailable: The environment could not be read.
env.lockedHint: A locked name is derived from how the server runs — the mode, the domain, the language set, the way sign-in is wired. Editing it by hand would put it out of step with what is configured elsewhere, and what breaks is not this page but the way in. Change these through their own pages.
env.secretHint: An empty secret field means “leave unchanged”.
env.removeConfirm: Remove {key}? A service that expects it may stop working.
env.helpLabel: What these values are, and when they take effect
env.helpWhen: Most values are read by a service when it starts, so a save is only half the work — the service has to be restarted to see it. That is why the dedicated pages restart what they change and this one does not: here you may be editing anything, and restarting everything on every save would be worse than making you do it deliberately.
env.helpBuildTitle: Some values are baked at build time.
env.helpBuild: Anything beginning with NEXT_PUBLIC_ is compiled INTO the application, not read at runtime. Changing it here does nothing until the next deploy — the running application still carries the old value. This surprises people often enough to be worth stating plainly.
env.helpMaskTitle: Why secrets show as a mask.
env.helpMask: A value whose name contains KEY, SECRET, TOKEN or PASSWORD is masked on the server and never sent to your browser. You can replace it; you cannot read it back. There is nothing to gain from looking at a key you already own, and plenty to lose from having it sit in a page.
env.helpLockedTitle: Why some names cannot be edited.
env.helpLocked: Their values follow from decisions made elsewhere — the mode the server runs in, the domain, the language set. A hand-edit here would rewrite one half of a pair and leave the other, and the failure would show up as “I cannot sign in” rather than “I mistyped a variable”.
env.exportHint: Working on this project from your own machine? Download the environment file: your local copy then reads and writes the SERVER's rows, files and vector memory through it. Nothing is copied to your laptop, so there are no two versions of the data drifting apart.
env.exportWarning: The file carries the data-layer key. Put it in the project root, never into git — the starter's .gitignore already excludes it.
env.keyTitle: Give your agent access to the server
env.keyLead: Your agent builds the project on the server and reads why something failed. To do that it needs a key — and the key is issued here, by you, in one click. Until you click, the agent has no way in: the environment file simply arrives without the access lines, and every attempt to build ends with a refusal.
env.keySteps: One button is enough: press .env.local on the left. The access key is created on the server, authorised there and travels inside that same file — you place nothing by hand. Save the file next to package.json in your clone and tell your agent it can deploy.
env.keyIssuedNote: The key is issued. Press again only to replace it — the previous one stops working.
env.keyMissingNote: The key has NOT been issued yet. Until it is, the environment file arrives without the access lines and your agent cannot reach the server.
env.transferLabel: I have already moved .env.local to my local machine
env.transferHint: Git never carries this file: .env, .env.local and .env.*.local are ignored on purpose, so keys cannot leak into a public repository. Downloading is not moving — put the file next to package.json in your local clone, then tick the box.
env.sshLead: This server is yours, and you can reach it directly over SSH — that is how your coding agent builds the project, restarts it and reads why something failed.
env.sshOpen: How the agent works with the server
env.sshTitle: Working with the server over SSH
env.sshWhy: Two channels serve this project and they do not replace each other. GitHub carries the code — pull and push. SSH carries state and control: build the project, reload it with pm2, see which process actually answers on the port, read the logs and the deployed commit. Through GitHub you cannot learn whether what you sent is alive; through SSH you cannot deliver a change into your repository.
env.sshAllowed: One folder — /opt/fractera/app. That is your project: your pages, your logic, your tables. Change it through pull and push rather than by hand on the server, so your repository stays the original.
env.sshForbiddenTitle: What must not be changed — and why it is not a prohibition.
env.sshForbidden: Everything in /opt/fractera outside app/ is the platform: authorisation, the data layer, this control panel, the services. Reading its code is useful and encouraged — a service answered oddly, open its handler. Editing it changes nothing that lasts: deployment runs rm -rf /opt/fractera and installs the platform again, so the edit does not survive the next deployment and is stored nowhere.
env.sshHowTitle: How to change what cannot be changed.
env.sshHow: Ask us. Name the service, the file and the line, and say whether a workaround exists. The button below writes the letter for you, with this server's address already in it — send it from your own mail.
env.servicesTitle: Values that live in the services
env.servicesLead: These do not sit in the environment file: the Telegram token and chat id belong to the channels service, the OpenAI key to the knowledge service. Shown here so you can check them without leaving the page.

appFeatures.intro: These switches apply without a rebuild — the app reads them on the next page load. Some of them also open and close a settings section of their own; each such switch says below it which section, and where in the menu to find it.
appFeatures.unavailable: The platform settings could not be read.
appFeatures.opensSection: Opens the “{section}” section, under “{group}” in the menu
appFeatures.parallelOff: Unavailable while parallel routing is on — there the layout decides the width.

topMenu.label: Top menu
topMenu.description: A navigation bar across the top of your app. Turn it off for a single screen that has nowhere to navigate to.

footerPages.label: Footer navigation links
footerPages.description: Links to your project's pages in the footer. Turn it off for a one-page site.

cookieBanner.label: Cookie notice
cookieBanner.description: The consent notice shown on a first visit. Required in the EU and the UK whenever you use analytics or any non-essential cookie — and pointless when you use none.

auth.label: Authorization in the main app
auth.description: Puts a sign-in button in the top right corner. Turn it on when the project has accounts or personal data; an ordinary landing page does not need it.

breadcrumbs.label: Breadcrumbs
breadcrumbs.description: A navigation trail on every page — it tells a visitor where in the project they are, and emits the structured markup search engines read for it.

faq.label: Question & answer section
faq.description: Reserves an area for questions and answers on every page. Close to mandatory on pages built from text content, and read by search engines.

themeToggle.label: Day / night theme switch
themeToggle.description: Lets the visitor choose light or dark instead of inheriting whatever their system decided.

widthToggle.label: Full screen width switch
widthToggle.description: Lets the visitor widen the central content to the full width of the screen.

languageSwitcher.label: Language switcher in the footer
languageSwitcher.description: Lets a visitor pick the language themselves instead of taking the browser's guess — and keeps it on every page that follows.

socials.label: Social links in the footer
socials.description: The row of social icons at the bottom of the site. Which networks and which profiles is a separate setting — App settings; here you decide whether the row exists at all.

appFeatures.helpLabel: Why configure from here at all
appFeatures.helpDefaultTitle: By default the project is built from this panel.
appFeatures.helpDefault: A capability switched on here appears in the app on its own — you write no code for it, and the attributes of your project come together by choosing rather than by building.
appFeatures.helpFreedomTitle: You are not obliged to use it.
appFeatures.helpFreedom: Inside your own project you may ignore this layer entirely and implement everything yourself, from the top menu to the cookie notice. Nothing here forbids that, and nothing breaks if you do.
appFeatures.helpWhyTitle: But it is not what we would advise.
appFeatures.helpWhy: These settings are built so that the public layer stays static: pages are generated ahead of time, a search engine receives finished markup, and the server answers the minimum number of requests. A hand-written version of the same capability usually pulls the page into dynamic rendering — and that is exactly the advantage it costs you.
appFeatures.helpSections: Some switches own a settings page of their own, and each of them names it right below the switch. Turned off, that page leaves the menu: configuring a banner the app will never show is time spent on nothing.

items.languages: The language set is not confirmed — it decides the shape of every address
items.github: GitHub is not connected — the project has nowhere to live
items.env-local: The environment file has not been moved to your machine — the local copy cannot start without it
items.mode: The development mode has not been chosen — classic is running by default, and it decides what the whole project asks of you
items.products: No product is described yet — development has nothing to build towards
items.openai: No OpenAI key — the knowledge graph and embeddings stay off
items.domain: No custom domain — HTTPS-only features stay unavailable
items.context-state: An unfinished session is recorded — read it before building, or clear it
items.dev-browser: The agent cannot see the result of its work: console errors, behaviour without JS and the service worker are invisible in source.
items.dev-claude-code: Claude Code is not marked as installed — there is nobody to write the code this panel configures.
items.dev-editor: No editor is marked as installed — you have nowhere to see your project as a whole.
items.auth-bypass: Auth bypass is live in secure mode — site, panel and data are open to anyone

contextState.experimentalHint: Off by default and worth switching on deliberately: it is still finding its shape and may change. Switching it on also switches the rule on in the project's main instruction; switching it off disables the rule there.
contextState.createdDoc: Document created — it is now a file in your repository
contextState.createHint: This project has no CONTEXT-STATE.md yet: it was started before this capability existed. Create it from the template — the model fills it in by itself from then on.
contextState.noticeTitle: This is a notice, not a fault.
contextState.notice: A record here means the previous session ran out of room mid-work and left a note for the next one. That is often completely normal — it is how work survives a window ending.
contextState.how: When the context window reaches 75%, the model writes this handoff by itself: what it was doing, where it stopped and what the next action is. If the session is then lost, the next one starts from this page instead of from nothing.
contextState.staleTitle: If it no longer matches reality, clear it.
contextState.stale: The record says where the work was INTERRUPTED, not where it is now — the project may well have moved past it. A stale handoff is worse than none, because it sends the next session back to work that is already done. Delete the text and save; nothing breaks.

tools.intro: Small reusable pieces the panel uses for itself and hands to your project. Installing copies the files into your project — after that they are your code: edit them, rename them, throw them away.
tools.updateConfirm: This overwrites your copy and loses local edits.
tools.outdated: the panel's version has changed since

image-crop.title: Image crop
image-crop.body: Pick the visible part of a picture before it is saved: pan, zoom, fixed 16:9 / 1:1 / 9:16. Everything happens in the browser and the server receives a finished JPEG. The aspect can be locked where the shape is decided by purpose — a logo has to be square.

video-trim.title: Video trim
video-trim.body: Keep the middle of a clip and drop the rest. The browser picks the boundaries, the cut is made on the server, and the result replaces the stored object. Duration is measured after the fast pass rather than trusted, because a copy-cut lands on keyframes and silently returns a longer clip.

voice-input.title: Voice input
voice-input.body: A microphone button next to any text field: speech is transcribed and inserted at the cursor, so a long description is spoken instead of typed. Ships with its own interface strings in ten languages. Needs the OpenAI key, and a microphone is only offered by the browser over HTTPS.

code-view.title: Code view
code-view.body: Source code with real syntax colouring — the kind that understands the language rather than guessing at it: nested CSS inside HTML, generics in TypeScript, keys and strings in JSON all come out right. Detects the language from the file extension and covers what a front end is written in: html, css, scss, ts, tsx, js, jsx, json, md, yaml, sql, bash and more. Carries light and dark colours in the same markup, so switching theme recolours instantly instead of re-parsing.

translations-dialog.title: Translations dialog
translations-dialog.body: One card per language for any field with translations. Translate them all at once with a model, or write your own wording — each language saves on its own, so fixing two of ten does not touch the rest. An untouched card shows the source text, so it is clear what is being translated. Voice input in each card speaks that card's language. Refusals are named plainly and link to where they are fixed.

tools.helpCopy: Installing writes the tool's files into your project. Nothing is fetched from the panel at runtime, so the app keeps working whether the panel is there or not — and you are free to change the tool, which is what almost always happens.
tools.helpWhere: `tools/<name>/` in the project root, next to an INSTALLED.json recording the version and date. That file is how the panel later notices your copy has fallen behind.
tools.helpAgentTitle: What the agent does with them.
tools.helpAgent: The agent reads `tools/` and reuses what is there instead of writing the same thing again. `PLATFORM-TOOLS.md` tells it these tools exist, where they land and how to import them.
tools.helpUpdate: Installing a second time replaces the files with the panel's current version and loses local edits — which is why an update asks first and a first install does not.
tools.npmNeeded: This tool needs a package your project does not have yet. After installing the files, run {cmd} in the project — the tool will not build without it.
tools.helpDeps: Usually not. Three of the four tools use only what the starter already has — React, Next, lucide-react, sonner and the shadcn button — so installing the files is the whole job. Code view is the exception: syntax colouring needs the Shiki grammars, so it asks for one package, and its page says so before you install.

docsOverview.whyTitle: Why a project needs this many documents
docsOverview.whyLead: At first glance it looks like a lot of reading for a starter, and loading it into a model's context looks like a cost. That impression is worth taking seriously — and it holds in exactly one case.
docsOverview.whyOneEdit: It holds when you want a single small change. Then the context spent on the whole picture really is paid for nothing.
docsOverview.whyWhole: Most work is not that. Development means finding and changing a meaningful part of the code — and the larger an application grows, the higher the chance that a change in one place quietly breaks another. In that situation it is far more useful to hand the model a coherent picture: what already exists, how the parts are connected, how they work, and why they came to be this way. That picture is what these documents are.
docsOverview.whyModels: This also became true only recently. A year ago instructions of this kind could not carry their own weight. By mid-2026 models respond to a documented architecture very differently — they use it, and the work becomes both faster and cheaper by a wide margin.
docsOverview.whyExperience: Most of this documentation grows on its own as the project moves. The structure is not invented here: it comes from building projects well past a million lines of code, and it earned its place by keeping token spend low rather than by looking thorough.
docsOverview.evolvingExplained: The agent adds to these as the work goes on: a term that caused confusion, a lesson from a mistake, a step that was completed, a dead end not to repeat. You are not expected to maintain them — their growth is the record of the project thinking about itself.
docsOverview.staticExplained: These you or the platform write, and the agent obeys them. It edits them only when asked — otherwise it would be rewriting the rules it works by, which is exactly how an agent talks itself into the wrong build.
docsOverview.closing: A document that does not exist yet is not a mistake — it is simply work that has not been needed so far. Open one and it will tell you what belongs in it.

purposes.doc-context-state: What the previous session was doing when its context window ran out: where it stopped and what the next action is. The model writes it by itself and the next session reads it, so interrupted work resumes instead of restarting. Empty is its normal state — it holds something only between an interruption and a resumption.
purposes.doc-instruction: The rules of the work itself: how the agent talks to you, what it must read before building, what it may never touch. Everything else is read through this one.
purposes.doc-use-cases: What the product is for, in your words — who uses it, what they came to do, what has to be true when they are done. Development does not start before this exists: an agent that knows how to build but not what for will build carefully and build the wrong thing.
purposes.doc-platform-tools: What the platform already gives you: stores, vector search, the knowledge graph, the map, channels. The agent has no external tools, so this file is the only way it learns these exist — and not knowing is how a second database gets built next to the first.
purposes.doc-architecture: How this particular app is put together and which layer owns what. It grows with the project, so a later session can pick up a structure instead of re-deriving it from the code.
purposes.doc-glossary: The terms of this project, so one word keeps one meaning. Cheap to maintain and it removes a whole class of misunderstandings that otherwise cost a session each.
purposes.doc-lessons: Your preferences and the habits earned from earlier mistakes. A session ends and takes its context with it; this is the part that survives — say “remember this” and it goes here.
purposes.doc-steps: One database row per piece of work, written by whoever did it. The project history in a form the next session can use: what was tried, what was decided, what is already closed — answered by one query instead of reading every file.
purposes.doc-case-to-step: How confirmed use cases turn into a queue of development steps: who starts it, how a step is named, and who may confirm what. A readable duplicate — the procedure itself lives in a skill the agent loads on demand, not in every session.
purposes.doc-antipatterns: Approaches that cost time here and must not be tried again. The value is in the second half of each entry — not what failed, but why, so a similar idea can be recognised before it is built.
purposes.doc-design: How the pages should look. You describe it once; the agent builds to that description instead of inventing a look per page and leaving you to correct it afterwards.
purposes.doc-parallel-routing: How a page assembled from independent areas works in this project, and what changes when it is turned on. Read before touching layout, not after.
purposes.doc-coding-standards: The limits the code must respect: size before decomposition, static public pages, text through translations, settings read rather than hardcoded. They are limits, not style advice — reaching one is a signal to restructure.
purposes.doc-troubleshooting: Problems that appear only in production and their real causes. Loaded on demand rather than at session start: a diagnostic manual held in every session is paid for in every session, including the ones where nothing is broken.
purposes.doc-code-samples: Finished pieces of code and styles from your earlier projects. The agent does not look here on its own: ask it to use the samples and name the document — that is how your accumulated work becomes a starting point rather than a forgotten folder.
purposes.doc-testing: How a step is proven finished. Two independent proofs from two different planes, in a fixed shape — because the rule existed for a long time as a goal and kept losing to the cheapest available answer: a build log. Switched off, nobody is asked for proofs.
purposes.doc-single-agent: Multi-agent development is forbidden unless you activate it by voice or in writing with the command. A sub-agent starts cold: it does not have this conversation, your corrections or the reason the previous approach was dropped, so it re-derives them wrongly and you pay twice — for the tokens and for the review that finds the divergence.
purposes.doc-dialogue-format: Every answer opens by restating your request in the agent's own words — the subject, what will be done, what should come out, and an invitation to correct it. The cheapest instrument here: a misread request is found in one sentence, or after a day of building the wrong thing. It matters most because you speak your requests, and dictation drops words.
purposes.doc-passport: What the product consists of, and the state of each part. One row per entity: what it is for, which cases it serves, which platform tools it needs, whether it is empty, in progress or working. It is the join between the cases and the steps — coverage runs case → entity → step, which is more honest than counting closed steps.

It also carries the law of the two links — external ones always absolute, and one internal link home per language, signed with your site name. Every rule here is enforced by npm run check:content, so a new post cannot repeat a mistake an old one made.

parallelRouting.intro: These settings live in a file on your server and apply WITHOUT a rebuild — a save shows up on the app's next page load.
parallelRouting.unavailable: The platform settings could not be read.
parallelRouting.notConsumed: Nothing reads this setting yet. The application does not implement parallel routing at the moment, so your choice is recorded in the platform config and applies once the application learns to read it. Saving here changes the file, not the screen.
parallelRouting.movesChildren: Turning parallel routing on moves the content of the children slot — the one ordinary routing renders — into the Center area. Interface elements that live above the page, such as drawers, modals and popovers, may need extra configuration afterwards.
parallelRouting.helpFormat: One of two shapes, never a third. Standard mode writes { "routingMode": "standard" } and no area map at all — describing a layout nobody lays out would be storing an untruth. Parallel mode writes { "routingMode": "parallel" } together with all eight areas, each explicitly true or false. A consequence worth knowing: turning parallel routing off drops the ticked set, so switching it back on starts from the default areas.
parallelRouting.saved: Saved — reload the app to see the layout
parallelRouting.appliesOnLoad: Areas apply on the app's next load
parallelRouting.routingOff: Parallel routing is off — the app renders the flat page tree
parallelRouting.helpLabel: Parallel routing — a page built from independent areas
parallelRouting.helpWhat: Instead of one page rendering everything, the screen is assembled from several named areas that render independently — a centre, a left and a right side, a promo screen above, a header and footer inside the centre. Each area has its own address, its own state and its own error boundary.
parallelRouting.helpShop: The centre carries the main subject — a catalogue, a product, or an AI chat. The right side shows the basket. The promo screen on top runs a campaign. The centre header recommends what sells best; the centre footer offers what goes with the item being viewed. Combining areas like this is where unusual applications come from — the same set of parts arranged differently is a different product.
parallelRouting.helpVsComponents: Components share the fate of the page they live on: one failure takes the whole screen, and one navigation re-renders everything. Areas do not. A failing area shows its own error and the rest of the page keeps working; each area navigates and keeps state on its own. The difference grows with size — it is decisive when an area has dozens or hundreds of pages of its own.
parallelRouting.helpStatic: That is the part people expect to lose. They do not: pages are still generated ahead of time, so delivery stays fast, cheap to serve and fully readable by search engines. Complex architecture, ordinary static output.
parallelRouting.helpFamiliar: Turn parallel routing off and work with a single-layer layout exactly as you are used to. Nothing else in the project depends on this choice.

languages.intro: These are the languages of YOUR site, not of this panel. They are baked in at build time, so saving starts a rebuild and takes two to four minutes.
languages.unavailable: The language settings could not be read.
languages.rebuildStarted: Saved — rebuilding to apply the languages (2–4 min)…
languages.rebuildDone: Rebuild finished — the languages are live
languages.rebuildFailed: The rebuild did not finish — the languages are not applied yet
languages.busyBuild: Another build is running — yours is queued behind it and will start on its own
languages.tierHint: Machine translation quality is lower for this language — check the result.
languages.howTitle: How languages work in your project
languages.howOne: Addresses carry no language at all: the home page is /, the rest are /about, /blog. The language switcher disappears on its own — there is nothing to switch between. This is the ordinary shape of a single-language site, and it is what most projects stay as.
languages.howMany: The language becomes the first part of every address — /en, /ru/blog — and the home page turns into one page per language. Each of them declares itself the original and names its translations, so a search engine keeps them apart instead of folding them into one.
languages.howSwitch: It happens by itself when you save: the mode follows the number of languages, there is no separate toggle. The set is baked at build time, so saving starts a rebuild of two to four minutes.
languages.howLangAttr: In both modes every page states its own language to browsers and screen readers — that never goes away, it simply stops being visible in the address.
languages.helpLabel: Why saving here rebuilds the application
languages.helpBuildTitle: Languages are baked in at build time.
languages.helpBuild: Every language becomes its own set of pages, generated once and served as files. That is what makes them fast and readable without JavaScript — and it is why a new language cannot appear until the application is built again. Writing the setting alone changes nothing visible.
languages.helpDefault: It is the one a visitor gets when their own language is not among yours, and the one a missing translation falls back to. It has to be one of the languages you selected — otherwise the site would point at pages it never built.
languages.helpEnglish: It is the last fallback for everything else, and an application with no language does not build at all.
languages.helpCost: Build time and disk, not money: every language multiplies the number of generated pages. Ten languages are ten copies of your site. Adding a language you do not serve pays that cost for nothing.
languages.readyLink: The expensive part is already built and tested — see what exactly
languages.fewerTitle: Take only as many languages as you really need
languages.fewerBody: Every language is a translation of every page — and of every page you add later. The more languages, the more time and money the texts cost you to keep.
languages.fewerBuild: Each page is also generated in as many versions as you have languages, so the build time of the project grows with the same multiplier.

appSettings.intro: These settings live in a file on your server, outside the repository. The application reads it on each request, so a save shows up on the next page load — no deploy needed.
appSettings.unavailable: The settings could not be read.
appSettings.baseLang: This is the base value — other languages fall back to it.
appSettings.helpLabel: Where these settings live and when they apply
appSettings.helpWhere: The file is deliberately not in git: it does not travel with a push or a pull, it is not in your local clone, and a fresh server runs on the code defaults until you save once. That is why changing branding in code is wrong twice — your change is not what the app reads, and it will be overwritten by the file that is.
appSettings.helpNoDeploy: The application reads the file on each request, so a save applies on the next page load. Only a MISSING field is a code matter, and that is a change to the platform rather than to your project.
appSettings.helpLangTitle: Why only five fields have languages.
appSettings.helpLang: A name, a description, a title template, keywords and a site name read differently in each language — the rest do not. A logo, a colour, a set of coordinates or an analytics id are the same in every language, and giving them a translation would be work with no result. Where a translation is missing, the base language is used.
appSettings.helpAgent: The file is not in the repository, so there is nothing for an agent on your machine to edit. If one offers to change branding or SEO in code, the answer is that those live here.

database.unavailable: The database could not be read. This is not the same as having no data.
database.noIdColumn: This table has no id column, so rows cannot be edited or deleted from here — only read.
database.helpLabel: The database — exact facts, compared with vector memory
database.helpHolds: Rows. Orders, customers, settings, prices — facts with a shape, where every value is exactly itself and nothing is approximate.
database.helpVsVectorTitle: How it differs from vector memory.
database.helpVsVector: A database answers questions you can state precisely: which orders shipped last week, how many are unpaid, what this customer spent. Vector memory answers questions you can only state loosely, by meaning. One is exactness over facts; the other is similarity over language. Asking the database "something about returns" gets you nothing; asking vector memory "sum of March invoices" gets you a paragraph that mentions March.
database.helpCost: Nothing per query, and no model is involved. Filtering, counting and sorting happen in milliseconds and stay exact however large the table grows.
database.helpWeak: It only answers what can be written as a query. It cannot find the passage that sounds like your question, and it has no opinion about meaning.
database.helpTogether: A vector record can point back at a row — its table and id travel with it. So a meaning-search over descriptions can end at the exact row, and the exact row can carry the text that made it findable. Same SQLite file, one backup, one wipe.

testing.why: The two-proof requirement lived in the pipeline as two lines for a long time and kept losing. Not because anyone disagreed — because it named the goal and left the form of the answer free, and a free form is always filled with the cheapest available proof: a build log, a 200, a commit hash. This document fixes the shape instead, so a missing proof is visibly missing.
testing.planes: A build and a type check are the same plane and count as one proof. Compilation is never one of the two: a build log looks identical whether or not the feature works. One of the proofs carries a negative control — a case whose answer is required to differ.
testing.switchWhere: On the documents map, together with the switches of every other instruction — the state of the whole corpus has to be readable from one screen.
testing.createdDoc: Document created — it is now a file in your repository
testing.createHint: This project has no TESTING.md yet: it was started before this document existed. Create it from the template.

singleAgent.why: A sub-agent starts cold. It does not have this conversation, your corrections, or the reason the previous approach was abandoned — so it re-derives them, and re-derives them wrong. What comes back reads like finished work resting on assumptions nobody agreed to.
singleAgent.planesTitle: What does NOT authorise a second agent.
singleAgent.planes: Not the size of the task, not "several independent parts", not "it would be faster in parallel". If the agent believes a second one is warranted, it says so in one sentence and keeps working alone.
singleAgent.switchWhere: Off means the guard is REMOVED, not forgotten: multi-agent work stops needing a command. The switch and the activation command both live on the documents map.
singleAgent.createdDoc: Document created — it is now a file in your repository
singleAgent.createHint: This project has no SINGLE-AGENT.md yet. Create it from the template.

dialogueFormat.why: You dictate most of your requests, and dictation drops words, merges sentences and mangles names. You see what you meant; the agent sees what the microphone produced. The restatement is where those two texts are compared — and the only place where comparing them is cheap. A misread request otherwise yields working code, a green build and a confident report about the wrong task.
dialogueFormat.shape: Four moves: the subject in the agent's own words · what will actually be done · what should come out, stated so it can be checked · an invitation to correct it. Said back as MEANING, never as a paraphrase of your wording — the same misunderstanding survives a paraphrase intact.
dialogueFormat.size: The block is sized to the request: a one-line ask gets a one-line restatement, a step gets the full form. The agent does not wait for your permission — it states and keeps working — and stops to ask only when two readings would produce materially different work.
dialogueFormat.switchWhere: On by default. Switched off, answers start directly and the agent does not apologise for it. The command asks for the restatement once, in full, even when the document is off — it means "stop and tell me how you understood me".

landing.title: Landing page
landing.definition: A single page with exactly one goal: to get a request or a contact. Everything on it serves that goal — the offer, the proof, the form. It never has a second goal, because two goals mean the visitor completes neither.
examples: A product launch behind paid advertising
A service page for a lawyer, doctor or tutor
Registration for a webinar or an event
Collecting pre-orders before production
signals: You pay for traffic and count the cost of one request
The sale happens in a conversation, not on the site
There is one product or one service — nothing to choose between
questions: The product and the offer: What exactly are you selling or presenting on this page — what does the person get and what are they paying for? And how does it work, from the moment a request comes in to the moment they get the result?

Audience and segments: Who is your target audience? Describe in detail every type of visitor (persona) who will land on the page: age, occupation, income level, where they live, what drives them, and how much they already know that a solution like yours exists.
The problem and the pain: What specific pain or task of the user does your product or service solve? What hurts most right now?

Your offer in one line: What makes your offer fundamentally different from the competition, and what headline with what promised advantage must the visitor see on the first screen within three seconds?

The main call to action: What is the one action a visitor should take (leave a request, buy in one click, download a file, book a demo, call you)? Describe the path you want them to walk to get there.
How you collect contacts: Which ways of getting in touch will the visitor have (a simple name-and-phone form, a multi-step quiz, a call-back widget, a jump into a Telegram bot)?

Required blocks: Which blocks must the page carry (hero, problem and solution, a 1-2-3 how-it-works, benefits, reviews, pricing, FAQ, cost calculator, closing call to action)? Say which come first, if the order matters.
Alternatives: How do people solve this problem today, when neither your product nor a competitor's is available to them?
The ideal outcome: From the user's point of view, what is the perfect end result — the one that leaves them completely satisfied?
Competitive landscape: Who are your direct and indirect competitors? Name the companies, their sites or landing pages you have seen — and say what you like about them and what you do not.
Proof and trust: What do you have to back the promise up (reviews, client logos, case studies, certificates, guarantees, hard numbers, press mentions)?
