Style and mood: What impression should the page leave (minimal, premium, bold, friendly, technical, expert)? Do you have references — links or descriptions of pages you like?
Integrations and analytics: Where should the collected data go (CRM, Telegram, email, a spreadsheet), and which analytics counters must be connected (Google Analytics, Yandex.Metrica, ad pixels)?
Languages and geography: Do you need several languages, automatic detection of city or currency, or content adapted to the region?

Technical and organisational constraints: Is there anything that has to be known upfront (A/B tests, required form fields, particular demands for the mobile version, a launch deadline, legal or industry restrictions)?

portfolio.title: Portfolio
portfolio.tagline: You are what is being chosen
portfolio.definition: A site where the thing being chosen is you: a specialist, a studio, a personal brand. What convinces is not a list of services but the work you show and the way you talk about it. So what matters most here is which projects you pick and the order in which they are seen.
examples: A designer, photographer or film editor
A small studio: development, architecture, interiors
An expert going after larger projects than the current ones
A specialist putting together an application for a dream job
signals: Clients choose you by looking at past work, not by reading a price list
You want projects of a particular kind, not just any
The price is agreed in conversation, and it depends on the impression you make
questions: Who you are and what you do: briefly — your profession, your specialisation, your experience, and how you work (freelance, a studio, an agency, a personal brand).
Your audience: who should be looking at this portfolio? Describe every type of person and company — prospective clients, employers, partners, investors — and what each of them needs you for.
What the portfolio is for: what should it bring you (enquiries, a higher rate, a particular kind of project, a personal brand, a job)?

Which work you show and how you choose it: which projects go up, how many, and in what form (case studies with the process explained, images or video, live links, before-and-after)? By what rule does a piece make it in, and what stays out? Remember: three strong pieces sell better than twenty assorted ones.

How a project is told: what must every case study contain (the client's task, the constraints, what exactly you did, the result in numbers, the client's words, the timeline and the team)? How much of the process do you reveal — or do you show only the outcome?

Sections and structure: which blocks must be there (home, about, projects and case studies, services, reviews, how you work, contacts, a blog)? Do you need a downloadable CV? Say which come first and in what order.

How people reach you and what follows: which ways of getting in touch are needed (a form, email, a messenger, booking a call in your calendar)? What happens after an enquiry — how quickly do you reply, what do you ask them to send, how does the first conversation end?
How people find you today: how do prospective clients or employers search for and judge specialists in your field, when they are not looking at your portfolio?
The ideal outcome: from the visitor's point of view, what is the perfect result of looking through it? What impression should they leave with, and what should they do next?
Who you look up to: whose portfolios do you take your bearings from — names, links? What do you like about them, and what is missing?
What sets you apart: what is the fundamental difference between you and other specialists or studios in your niche — the approach, the style, the results?
Your share of the work: in team projects, what did you do and what did your colleagues? How will that be stated, so that "I made this" does not come apart in the first conversation with a client?

Other people's rights and closed work: are there projects under a non-disclosure agreement or made under someone else's brand? May you name clients and show their logos? Do you need a closed part of the portfolio, opened by a link or a password?
What you do not show: is there work you can do but no longer want to? Niches and kinds of task you want the portfolio itself to filter out?
Style and mood: what visual character should the portfolio carry (minimal, premium, experimental, warm, technical, bold)? Do you have references you particularly like?
Proof: what do you want to show as evidence (client reviews, numbers you achieved, awards, publications, well-known clients, certificates)?

Money: do you state your price range or terms on the site — "from this amount", ranges for typical work, or only "let us discuss"? This decision filters out half the enquiries, and it should be made deliberately.
Being found and kept current: should people find you in search for your niche, or is the portfolio a card you send by link? Who will add new work after launch, and how often?

Technical and practical wishes: are there requirements or constraints (filtering projects by category, dark and light themes, several languages, links to outside work platforms, animation, the mobile version, updating the work yourself, a launch deadline)?

corporate.title: Corporate website
corporate.definition: A multi-page site of an organisation: directions, services, people, proof. It has no single call to action — it answers dozens of questions from different visitors.
examples: A manufacturer or a construction company
A clinic, a law firm, an engineering bureau
A B2B supplier with a long sales cycle
The site of an institution or a foundation
signals: The decision is made by several people and not in one visit
You are being checked: licences, track record, cases, the team
There are several directions, and each needs its own story
questions: What the company does: what is its business, what are the main product and service directions, and what mission do you want to convey? What exactly should the site present?
Audience: who are the main visitors? Describe every group — prospective clients, partners, investors, job seekers, journalists — and what each of them needs from the site.
The site's main job: what should it bring the company (inbound enquiries, trust in the brand, hiring, an official presence, supporting the sales team)? If one job matters most, name it.

Site map: which sections are required (about the company and its history, services and directions, projects and case studies, the team, a press centre, careers, contacts and offices, a client account)? Say which come first, if the order matters.

Services and products in detail: how deeply is each service described — can a presentation or a proposal be downloaded, a quote requested for a specific task, the make-up of a complex service and its pricing be seen?

Where enquiries go: where should requests, proposal enquiries and job applications land (a corporate CRM, an accounting system, a particular department's mailbox, a message to whoever is responsible)?

Who fills the site: who will add news and vacancies after launch — the company's marketer, a contractor, nobody? Do you need a simple page builder and a separation between those who write and those who publish?
What the client gets: what pain or need does the company close for those who come to it? What does a person get by choosing you?

How people find you today: how does your audience find companies in your field and decide to work with them, when not through a website (direct sales, trade shows, recommendations, tenders, industry platforms)?
The ideal outcome: what impression should a visitor leave with, and what should they do, for you to consider the site working?
Competitors and benchmarks: whose sites in your industry do you consider exemplary? Name the companies and links — and say what you like about them and what you find unsuccessful.
What sets the company apart: what is your advantage over competitors (approach, experience, results, expertise, scale, a narrow specialisation)?
Careers and vacancies: do you need a section for applying (filtering by city and department, uploading a CV, a link to outside hiring platforms or an internal recruitment system)?
Press centre and publications: do you need to publish news, articles, reports, a press kit and a newsletter sign-up? How often will this be updated?
Proof: what do you want to show to confirm your standing (case studies, reviews, hard numbers, well-known clients, awards, certificates, press coverage)?
Style and tone: what impression should the site convey (expert, premium, modern, formal, friendly, innovative)? Do you have references you like?
Languages and regions: do you need several languages, and a choice of office or branch depending on where the visitor comes from?

Security and requirements: are there particular requirements for the data and the site's operation (handling personal data and consent for it, where the servers are located, protection against mass attacks, a launch deadline)?

media.title: Media and blog
media.definition: A project whose value is regular material. It grows by pages and by search traffic; its machinery is sections, authors, a feed and search.
examples: An industry outlet or a news portal
An expert blog of a company
A personal blog with a paid subscription
A knowledge base of reference articles
signals: Material comes out regularly, not once
Traffic arrives from search and recommendations
The reader has to be held until the next piece
questions: The kind of project and its job: what are you making (a personal blog, a themed publication, a news site, an expert journal, a podcast platform, a blog alongside your main business)? And what should it bring — an audience, money, a name, support for the main business, a community?

Topics and formats: what will you write about and in what form (short news, long analyses, reviews, guides, interviews, video, podcasts, letters to subscribers)? Which sections matter most and how deep do the pieces go?
Audience: who are your readers? Describe every type — how deep they are in the subject, age, occupation, what concerns them — and why they will come back to you specifically.

Who writes and how often: who creates the material — you personally, an in-house team, invited authors, the readers themselves, help from a model? How many pieces a week can you realistically publish, and who takes over when you run out of time?
Sections and search: how does a reader find what they want (a hierarchy of sections, tags, editor's collections, special projects, what is being read right now, search across the site)?
How an article reads: what must be in the piece itself (reading time, a table of contents with jumps, a spoken version, footnotes and pull quotes, galleries, callouts, a dark theme)?

Monetisation: how does the project earn (advertising and sponsored pieces, a paid subscription for part of the articles, donations to authors, sponsored projects, selling your own goods)? What stays free forever?
The problem and the pain: what shortage of information do you close (no decent analysis in the niche, no independent view, industry news arriving as a stream with no meaning)?
How they read today: where does your audience get this kind of material now (messenger channels, social networks, video platforms, competing publications, newsletters)?
The ideal outcome: what experience turns a chance visitor into a regular reader? What habit do you want to form — coming daily, waiting for a weekly letter, reading everything you publish?
Competitors and models: which publications and platforms do you take your bearings from? Name them with links, and say what you like and what is missing in them.
What sets you apart: the angle, the format, the depth, the delivery, the expertise, the regularity?
Recommendations and links between pieces: how is the "read next" block assembled (by shared tags, by what others read, a personal feed for a signed-in reader)? How clever must this be at launch?
Community and engagement: do you need threaded comments, reactions, bookmarks, ratings of pieces, author reputation, sharing? Who moderates it and how?

Reach and distribution: what is needed to grow (sitemaps and social-network markup, subscription feeds, automatic announcements to messengers and social networks, letters to subscribers)? What share of the audience should arrive from search?

The editorial workplace: what do the people who publish need (scheduling a piece for later, a comfortable text editor, two people working on one draft, comment moderation, a split of roles — author, editor, proofreader)?
Style and mood: what should the publication look like (formal and businesslike, warm and personal, bold, academic, minimal)? Are there examples you like?
Technical and practical constraints: is there anything to be known upfront (an installable app, several languages, the traffic you expect, a launch deadline, who will run the site after launch)?

directory.title: Catalogue and directory
directory.definition: A collection of objects of one kind with filters, search and often a map. Its value is completeness and accuracy; every object gives a page of its own.
examples: A directory of a city's organisations
A catalogue of specialists or craftsmen
A database of properties
A listing of venues and events
signals: There are hundreds or thousands of objects and they are alike
People arrive asking «what is near me» or «who fits»
The data goes stale and has to be refreshed
questions: What is catalogued: what exactly goes into the directory (companies and venues, suppliers, specialists and doctors, places, products, digital tools, people, objects of a particular industry)? How many entries do you expect in the first year?
The audience on both sides: who searches and who wants to be listed? Describe those who use the search and those whose cards live here — business owners, specialists, representatives.

What the directory is for: what should a person get (find the right thing fast, compare options, trust the data, choose a provider)? What shortage do you close — no single base in the niche, information scattered, nowhere to find honest reviews?
The structure: how is navigation arranged (sections and subsections, tags, links between entries, neighbouring categories)? By what property does a person usually start searching?

The entry card: which fields are compulsory (name, images, contacts, address) and which are particular to your niche (opening hours, price band, payment methods, licences and certificates, languages served, capacity)? These same fields become the filters.

Search and filtering: how does a person find what they need (live search by name and synonyms, filtering by dozens of properties at once, sorting by rating, popularity or newness, comparing several entries, favourites)?

Where the data comes from: what fills the base at launch and afterwards (entered by an administrator, collected automatically from open sources, companies submit themselves, imported as a ready list)? Who checks a new entry, and by what rules?
How they search today: where do people find and compare such things without your directory (search engines, topic chats, friends, their own spreadsheets, other directories)?
The ideal outcome: what does the flawless case look like — a person found the right entry with exact contacts and prices in ten seconds and made an informed choice? What has to be on screen for that?
Competitors and models: which directories and catalogues do you take your bearings from? Name them with links, say what you like and what is missing.
What sets you apart: depth of data, ease of search, freshness, a narrow specialisation, extra capabilities?
Map and geography: is there a tie to location (entries on a map, searching near me, filtering by district, city or station)? Or is geography irrelevant here?

Keeping data current: how does the directory avoid becoming a graveyard of dead phone numbers? Who updates entries and how often, what happens to those nobody has confirmed in a year, and can a visitor report an error?
Claiming a card: do you need a "this is my company" flow — confirming the right, editing contacts, replying to reviews, buying promotion? How do you verify the person really owns it?

Reviews and credibility: how are ratings arranged (an overall star score, detailed reviews with photos, scoring on separate criteria)? How are paid-for and vengeful reviews filtered out — pre-moderation, proof that the person was actually a customer, a right of reply?

Monetisation: how does the directory earn (paid listing or a subscription for companies, lifting an entry in the results and highlighting the card, advertising, selling the enquiries a card generates, paid access to extended data)? What stays free forever?

Pages built for search queries: should pages be generated automatically at the intersection of properties — of the kind "this thing in that city with that condition"? For directories this is the main source of visitors and also the main source of empty pages: how do you avoid creating the ones with nothing behind them?

Technical and practical requirements: is there anything to be known upfront (the size of the base, languages, a mobile version, links to outside data sources, who will moderate after launch, deadlines)?

booking.title: Booking and appointments
booking.definition: A project that sells an occupied interval: an appointment, a table, a room, a car, a hall. The core entity is not a product but the schedule of a resource.
examples: A salon, a clinic, a barbershop
Renting flats, cars or equipment
A restaurant and its table reservations
A coach, a tutor, a consultant
signals: Two people cannot take the same slot
Cancellations and no-shows cost you money
The schedule today lives in a notebook, a chat or a spreadsheet
questions: What is booked: what exactly does the client take (a specialist's personal time, a room or equipment, a table or a seat, a hotel room, a place at an event, an online consultation)? One kind of resource or several at once?

Both sides: who books and who receives bookings? Describe each side — clients and those providing the service: practitioners, doctors, administrators, the owner. Which of them will work in the system every day?

The pain on each side: what do you solve for the client (cannot get through by phone, booking is awkward, no way to see what is free) and for the receiving side (bookings scattered across chats, empty slots from no-shows, two bookings for one time, reminders by hand)?

The booking flow: how does it run from choosing to confirming (picking the service, the specialist or the resource, the date and time, extra requests, confirmation, payment)? What does the person see afterwards — their upcoming and past visits, rebooking in one tap, the chance to leave a review?

Slots and schedules: how is available time formed (a fixed length or one per service, working hours and breaks, a gap between clients for cleaning or preparation, each practitioner's own schedule, days off and holidays, several rooms or chairs)?

Money at booking: is payment needed upfront (full payment online, a non-refundable deposit against no-shows, holding an amount on the card, paying on arrival)? What happens to that money when either side cancels?

Cancellations, moves and no-shows: until when may a client cancel or reschedule themselves? Is there a limit on rescheduling and a penalty for cancelling late? What happens to the slot when it is freed — is it offered to someone, and to whom?
How they book today: how does it happen without your system (calling the front desk, messaging on a messenger, a paper diary, another service that did not fit)?
The ideal outcome: what booking experience makes the client happy with how simple it was, and rids the business of empty slots? Describe it from both sides.
Competitors and models: which services do you take your bearings from? Name them with links, say what you must have from how they work and what you consider unnecessary.
What sets you apart: convenience, flexible scheduling, automation, knowing your industry, price, connections to other systems?

Group bookings: should several people share one slot — a class of ten, a hall rented by a company, two clients seen at once? How is the remaining capacity counted, and what happens when the group does not fill?

Reminders: through which channels and how far ahead should reminders go (a messenger, SMS, email, a notification in the app)? Should the reminder carry "confirm" and "cancel" buttons, and what happens when the client does not answer?
Personal calendars: do you need two-way synchronisation with the calendars of practitioners and rooms, so that time taken by private matters closes itself for booking?
Branches and time zones: does the system work across several locations or cities? Should times be shown in the client's own zone — for online consultations this decides everything?

The staff workplace: how do employees see the bookings (a day and week grid, a list of statuses "expected — arrived — finished", a client card with visit history, links to the till and the customer records)? Who is allowed to change someone else's bookings?

Technical and practical constraints: is there anything to be known upfront (an installable app, languages, connections to payment services and accounting systems, the number of bookings you expect a day, a launch deadline, who will run the system)?

qr-menu.title: Digital menu
qr-menu.tagline: A table, a phone and the kitchen
qr-menu.definition: A menu the guest opens on their own phone at the table. One decision defines the product: does it only show the dishes, or does it take the order and the payment? In the second case a till, a kitchen, a table number and a stop list grow onto it at once — and it stops being a shop window and becomes part of how the place runs.
examples: A menu behind a code on the table instead of a laminated folder
Ordering and paying from the phone without waiting for a waiter
A chain's menu where prices and stop lists differ per venue
A menu for a tourist spot where half the guests read no Russian
signals: Prices change more often than you are willing to reprint
A guest waits for the waiter longer than they choose a dish
A dish runs out in the kitchen while the menu still offers it
questions: What the product is and how far it goes: only showing dishes behind a code on the table, taking the order, or taking the order and the payment straight from the guest's phone? Half the remaining answers depend on this.

The venue and the kitchen: what format (a restaurant with tablecloths, a café, a bar, a coffee shop, fast food, a food court, a chain) and what cuisine? What sets the place apart from the one next door?
The guests: who visits you? Describe them — how they arrive, how long they stay, in company or alone, how used they are to ordering from a phone, how many are visitors from elsewhere.

Structure and navigation: how is the menu arranged (sections and subsections, the order of dishes, seasonal items, sets and combos, search, filtering by things like "no meat" or "spicy")? How many items in total?

The dish card: what do we show the guest (a photo or video, ingredients, allergens, calories and weight, how spicy, cooking time) and what options do they choose — how it is cooked, the sauce, the portion size, a milk substitute, paid extras?

Stop list and prices: how does an item disappear when the kitchen has run out — by hand from the panel, or by itself from the stock data? Who changes prices, and how quickly does the guest see the change?
The till and the kitchen: should the order land in the venue's till system by itself and print or appear on the kitchen and bar screens? Which system do you use today?

What the menu is for: what should it give the venue (showing dishes conveniently, a bigger bill, faster ordering, less load on the waiters, no reprinting costs when prices change, removing the language barrier)?
How it works today: how does a guest read the menu and order without your solution (a paper folder, a board at the counter, calling a waiter, somebody else's digital menu)?
The ideal outcome: what experience would delight the guest, raise the average bill and turn tables faster? Describe it through the guest's eyes and the manager's.
Competitors and models: which solutions do you take your bearings from? Name them with links, say what you like most and what is missing.
What sets you apart: the look, the convenience, how fast it opens, how easy it is to update, the depth of features, being built for one kind of venue?

Tables and ordering scenarios: how does the system know where the order came from (a code per table, a zone or terrace, takeaway, ordering for a set time)? Do you need "call the waiter" and "bring the bill" buttons?
Payment, tips and splitting the bill: how does the guest pay (card, instant transfer, paying the waiter)? Do you need to split the bill between people at one table and leave a tip for the waiter?
Languages: how many languages are needed, and should the language be picked from the guest's phone by itself? Who translates the dish names — you or the system?
Upselling: how does the menu raise the bill ("often taken with this", sets, dish of the day, offers by time of day, extras on the card)? Where is that welcome and where would it annoy?
The staff workplace: do the waiters and the kitchen need a screen (calls from tables, new orders and confirming them, the state of the room)? Which staff may change the stop list and prices?

Technical and practical constraints: is there anything to be known upfront (working on a weak signal in the room, an installable app or only a page behind a code, a dark look, who will maintain the menu after launch, deadlines)?

store.title: Online store
store.definition: A shop window for goods that belong to you, with a cart, payment and delivery. There is one seller — you; the buyer picks from your stock and pays on the site.
examples: Your own clothing or cosmetics brand
A shop attached to a production line
Digital goods: files, keys, access codes
A grocery shop with city delivery
signals: Items repeat: the same product is sold many times
You have stock levels and they change
The order is placed on the site, even when payment happens on delivery
questions: Range and business model: What exactly are you selling — categories, roughly how many products, are there variants (size, colour, configuration)? And how does the shop work: your own stock, dropshipping, a place for other sellers, or made to order?

Audience and segments: Who are your buyers? Describe every key type — retail and wholesale, private people and companies, impulse and considered purchases — along with age, income, where they live, and how often they buy things like this.

The problem and the pain: What is the main thing your shop solves for the buyer (a range no one else has, a better price, speed of delivery, ease of choosing)? Why should they buy from you and not elsewhere?

Catalogue structure and the product page: How deep do the categories nest? Which attributes and variants must a product carry (size, colour, configuration, gallery, video)? Are the goods physical, digital, or both?

The buyer's path, cart and checkout: How does a person get from the first visit to payment? What checkout do you need — one-click purchase, a multi-step checkout, ordering without registration, an account with order history?
Payment: Which payment methods and services must be connected (bank cards, instant transfers, instalments and pay-in-parts, cryptocurrency, cash on delivery, an invoice for companies)?

Delivery and geography: How is delivery calculated and arranged (your own couriers or delivery services, pickup points and collection in person, choosing a city and a country, cost by weight and size, shipping abroad)?
Alternatives: Where and how do buyers get goods like yours today, when your shop is not there (ordinary shops, marketplaces, classified ads, ordering from abroad)?
The ideal outcome: What is the perfect buying experience from the customer's point of view — the one that brings them back?
Competitive landscape: Who are your main competitors? Name the companies and links to their shops or marketplaces — and say what you like about them and what irritates you.
What sets you apart: what is your main difference from the competition (the range, prices, service, speed, expertise, exclusivity, the way you treat customers)?
Search, filters and sorting: How does a buyer find what they need (smart search with suggestions, filters by attribute, tag and price, sorting, comparing products side by side)?

Stock and availability: Where does availability data come from (typed into the panel by hand, synchronised with an accounting system, imported from a file, live stock levels)? What happens when an item runs out while an order is being placed?
The customer account and service: What does a person need once signed in (order history, favourites, product reviews and ratings, live chat, reordering in one tap)?
Marketing and retention: Do you need discount mechanics (promo codes, accumulating bonuses, a loyalty programme, struck-through prices, countdown offers, abandoned-cart emails)?
Notifications and integrations: Where and how should order status reach the buyer and the manager (push, SMS, a Telegram bot, email, passing the order into a CRM)?
Style and mood: What impression should the shop leave (premium, minimal, bright and young, expert, cosy, technical)? Do you have references you like?
Proof and trust: What do you want to show as evidence (reviews, ratings, number of sales, well-known customers, certificates, guarantees, press mentions)?

Technical, legal and practical constraints: Is there anything that has to be known upfront (several languages, several currencies, mandatory certification or product labelling, a launch deadline, who will fill the catalogue and how)?

learning.title: Courses and learning
learning.definition: A project where a person walks a path: lessons, assignments, progress, access. What is sold is not a file but being carried to a result.
examples: An online school or an expert's course
Corporate training for employees
A membership club with materials
Preparation for an exam
signals: The material has an order, and the order matters
You can see where each person stopped
Access opens and closes rather than being granted forever
questions: What kind of educational product: what are you building (your own online courses, a platform for other authors, a school with several tracks, training for a company's staff, a mentoring programme, interactive practice tools)?
Topics and level: what do you teach and for whom — a beginner, a practitioner, an expert? How deep do you go, and how many courses do you plan in the first year?

Both sides: who learns and who teaches? Describe the students — age, background, what drives them (changing profession, a hobby, an exam, an employer's demand) — and the authors and tutors, if they are not only you.

How material is delivered: in what form does it come (recorded video lessons, long texts, live meetings, short daily sessions of a few minutes, practice tools that check you on the spot)? Which of these is primary and which supports it?

When lessons open: access to the whole course right after payment, strictly by date, the next lesson after the previous is passed, or learning in cohorts with a common start? The shape of the entire course depends on this.

Homework and marking: how is knowledge checked (multiple-choice tests, work uploaded for a tutor, written pieces, automatic checking of code or tasks by a model)? Who marks it, and within what time must they answer?

How access is sold: buying a course once and forever, a subscription to the whole library, paying in instalments, selling separate modules, free first lessons, a contract with a company for its staff? If it is a platform for other authors — what share do you take?
The student's pain: what problem do you solve (people drop out halfway through other courses, no practice, the programme is out of date, it costs too much, nobody to go through mistakes with)?
How they learn today: where do people get this knowledge without you (videos and books, a private tutor, in-person courses, other platforms, not at all)?
The ideal outcome: how should the learning end for a person to call it a success (an exam passed, a portfolio built, a job, a named certificate, simply confidence)?
Competitors and models: which platforms and schools do you take your bearings from? Name them with links, say what you like and what is missing.
What sets you apart: the method, the way material is delivered, the support, how much practice there is, the community, the result at the end, the price?
Roles in the system: who is needed besides the student (course author, marking tutor, curriculum designer, administrator, a representative of the client company) and what may each of them do?
Video and protecting the material: where does the video live, and does it need protecting from downloading and resharing? What other formats are needed — documents, audio, slides, downloadable files?

Communication and support: how does a student ask a question (comments under the lesson, a group chat for the cohort, private messages with a tutor, a forum, a messenger group)? Who answers, and how quickly?

Retention and completion: do you need a progress bar, points and achievements, deadlines, reminders for those falling behind, a table of the group's results? What do you do with someone who quit halfway?

Certificates and the author's reports: do you need a named certificate with a verifiable number? What summaries do you need as the owner (how many finished, where people most often quit, average marks, how loaded the tutors are)?

Technical and practical constraints: is there anything to be known upfront (a course builder for authors, languages, links to payments and customer records, an installable app, how many students you expect at once, a launch deadline)?

tours.title: Tours marketplace
tours.tagline: A place, a date and the person who will show you
tours.definition: A platform where a traveller looks for an experience on a particular day in a particular city, and a guide receives a confirmed booking with no messaging. It rests on three things at once: geography, the calendar, and money between two sides. Separate from a marketplace and from booking — because here there is weather, a season, and an unfamiliar city.
examples: Walks around the city led by the people who live there
A tour agency tired of running bookings through chat
The experiences of one region: mountains, sea, food
Workshops and live events for visitors
signals: A person searches not for a product but for "what to see here on these dates"
Every offer has its own host and its own schedule
A tour may not happen because of the weather, and nobody is to blame
questions: What is aggregated: which tours and experiences will the platform carry (on foot and by transport, private and group, single-day and multi-day, for children, adventurous, workshops, online meetings)? Is there a specialisation — a city, a country, a theme?

Both sides: who travels and who hosts? Describe each side — travellers (alone, families, the premium end, visitors or locals) and organisers (private guides, agencies, guides who speak other languages).

The pain on each side: what do you solve for the traveller (hard to choose, afraid of being cheated, unclear whether it will happen) and for the guide (no steady stream, bookings lost in chat, time gone to arranging)?

The traveller's path: how does it run from search to the tour itself (search and filtering, the offer's page, choosing a date, booking, payment, confirmation and a voucher, a reminder the day before, a review afterwards)? Do you need favourites and messaging with the guide beforehand?

The guide's calendar and prices: how does an organiser run their schedule (available days and hours, a gap between tours, a different number of places, a higher price in season and at weekends, closing dates by hand)?
How a booking is confirmed: instantly with immediate payment, or does the guide confirm within an agreed time? What happens when they never answer, and does the traveller see that waiting?
How the platform earns: commission on a booking, a subscription for organisers, paid promotion in the results, advertising? Who pays the commission — the traveller, the guide, or both?
How they find it today: where does a traveller get a tour without your platform (the hotel desk, touts on the street, ads on social networks, friends, the big aggregators)?

The ideal outcome: what does the flawless case look like — the traveller found the right thing for the right date in two moves, the guide got a confirmed booking without a single message? Describe it from both sides.
Competitors and models: which platforms do you take your bearings from? Name them with links, say what you like most and what is missing.
What sets you apart: a narrow theme, how carefully guides are chosen, convenience, price, unusual formats, a strong focus on particular cities or countries?

Search, map and filters: how does a person find what they want (by city, country or landmark, on a map with meeting points, filtering by date, price, length, language of the tour, format)? What do you show someone who has not chosen a city yet?

How money moves: how is it settled (paid fully online and passed to the guide after the tour, a part upfront and the rest on the spot, everything on the spot)? When does the guide get paid, and what is held back during a dispute?

The organiser's workplace: what does a guide need (adding and editing programmes, photos and video, their own schedule, the list of people booked for a given date, messaging the traveller, withdrawing earnings, reports)?

Trust and quality: how are guides selected and how is trust built (checking documents and permits, reviews only after a tour that took place, ratings in both directions, handling complaints, removing someone from the platform)? Who checks a newcomer?

Cancellations, weather and force majeure: what are the refund rules when the traveller cancels (a day before, an hour before, on the day)? What happens when the guide cancels, and what when the weather is to blame — that is, nobody? Is there a penalty for a guide who does not show up?

Notifications and connections: what must be connected (maps, messages to traveller and guide about the upcoming meeting and any changes, currency conversion, organisers' calendars)? How far ahead should the reminder go?

Technical, geographic and practical constraints: is there anything to be known upfront (launch cities and countries, languages and currencies, an installable app, payment services and the legal form of settling with guides, a launch deadline, who will run the platform)?

delivery.title: Delivery service
delivery.tagline: Customer, courier and venue — three to an order
delivery.definition: A platform where every order has three sides: the one who ordered, the one who carries it, and the one who hands it over. Everything rests on the map and the clock — where the courier is now, how long they will take, what it costs. A mistake in how orders are handed out costs more than any mistake in layout.
examples: Hot food delivered from several venues
Groceries and goods from shops nearby
Courier delivery of documents and parcels across the city
A chain's own delivery arm, tired of somebody else's commission
signals: An order has someone who carries it, and that someone has to be assigned
The customer wants to watch their order move on a map
The price depends on distance, weight or the time of day
questions: The kind of service: what exactly do you deliver and in what form (hot food, groceries and goods from shops, documents and parcels, consolidated freight, door-to-door courier work, a logistics platform for business)? Within one city, between cities, or both?

The three sides and what each can do: who uses the system — customers, couriers (on foot, by bike, by car), venues and shops, dispatchers, support? Describe every side and exactly what it is allowed to do.

The problem and the pain: what is the main problem the service solves (slow delivery, high price, no oversight of couriers, poor routes, lost orders)? What irritates people most today — the customer, the courier, or the venue?

The life of an order: what stages does an order pass from creation to completion (created, confirmed, being prepared, courier assigned, on the way, delivered)? Who creates it, how is delivery confirmed, and what happens on a cancellation, a delay, or a refusal at the door?

Assigning the courier: how does a courier get an order — automatically to the nearest free one, an open board where the first to take it wins, or by hand through a dispatcher? What happens when nobody takes it?

Maps and location: what map work is needed (the courier live on the map, resolving the address from the device's location, building a route, delivery zones and their borders, travel time allowing for traffic)?
Working out the delivery price: how is the price to the customer formed (a flat rate, distance, weight and size, time of day, surge demand, free delivery above a certain order value)?

Alternatives: how do people and companies send and receive orders today, when your service is not there (other delivery firms, their own couriers, collection in person, the post, an arrangement over a messenger)?
The ideal outcome: what delivery scenario do you consider perfect — one where all three come out ahead: the customer, the courier and the business?
Competitors and peers: who are you taking your bearings from? Name the services and links, say which of their features you must have, and what you consider their weak spot.
What sets you apart: what is your main difference from the competition (speed, price, unusual delivery zones, how you work with couriers, features nobody else has)?
How the service earns: where does your own revenue come from (commission on the order, commission from the venue or the courier, a subscription, a placement fee, advertising, paid priority delivery)?
Payments and settlements: how does money move (paid on the site or in the app, cash to the courier, tips, invoicing for companies, payouts to couriers and venues — how often and to where)?

Interfaces and devices: in what form does each side work (a site for the customer, an installable app, a separate courier app with notifications, a tablet or panel for the venue, a dispatcher's workstation)?

Key features: what must be there (live tracking on the map, choosing a delivery time, chat with the courier, ratings and reviews, repeating a past order, a loyalty programme, notifications at every stage)?
Integrations: what must the service connect to (mapping services, the venues' till and accounting systems, payment services, SMS and Telegram, a CRM)?
Style and mood: what impression should the site and the app leave (fast and technical, friendly and simple, premium, young)? Do you have references you like?

Technical, geographic and practical constraints: is there anything to be known upfront (which cities and zones you launch in, installable apps, how couriers are engaged, the load you expect at peak hour, a launch deadline, who will staff the dispatch desk)?

marketplace.title: Marketplace
marketplace.definition: A platform where other people sell. You have two kinds of users — seller and buyer — and you earn on the deal between them, not on goods of your own.
examples: A classifieds board for a city or a niche
A platform of craftsmen and customers
A shop window shared by several stores
An exchange for services or rentals
signals: The goods or services are not yours
Sellers must be attracted separately from buyers
There is a commission, moderation and disputes
questions: What is traded: what exactly is sold on the platform (physical goods, digital files, services and commissioned work, renting things or spaces, tickets, classified ads)? One category or several at once?
Both sides: who sells and who buys? Describe each side separately — who these people or companies are, what they do, how used they are to platforms like this.

The pain on each side: what problem do you solve for the buyer (no choice, no guarantees, hard to compare) and what for the seller (a high barrier to entry, no customers, trouble taking money)? Answer for both — they are different pains.

The deal: how does it run from search to completion (found, chose, messaged the seller, paid, received, confirmed, left a review)? Where do the two sides need to talk, and at which steps does safety matter most?
How the platform earns: commission on each deal, a listing fee, a subscription for sellers, paid promotion in the results, extra services? Who pays — the seller, the buyer, or both?

How money moves: whose account does it pass through (the platform holds it until receipt is confirmed, payment goes straight to the seller, part is held as a deposit)? When does the seller get paid, and what happens to the money during a dispute?

Trust and verification: how is trust built between strangers (reviews in both directions, checking the seller's documents, a "verified" mark, guarantees from the platform, moderating listings)? Who checks a new seller, and when?
How they find each other today: where do buyer and seller meet without your platform (social networks, classified boards, direct arrangements, agents and intermediaries, the big marketplaces)?
The ideal outcome: what does a flawless deal look like, where the buyer got what they wanted, the seller earned, and the platform took its share? Describe it through both pairs of eyes.
Competitors and models: which platforms do you take your bearings from — the giants or the narrow ones? Name them with links, say what you like and what you find weak.
What sets you apart: a narrow niche, better matching, the size of the commission, convenience, trust, extra services?
The seller's workplace: what do they need (managing their own catalogue and prices, stock and orders, a sales summary, withdrawing what they earned, reports for their accounts)?
The buyer's account: what do they see (favourites, purchase history, tracking orders from DIFFERENT sellers at once, a cart holding items from several sellers, reordering)?

Search and matching: how does a buyer find what they want (filters by price, rating and availability, search on a map and by distance, suggestions of similar offers, sorting)? By what rule are the offers ordered?

Disputes and refunds: how are conflicts resolved (a complaint, a review with support involved, refund scenarios, holding the payout while a dispute runs)? Who makes the final decision, and by what rules?

Delivery and fulfilment: how does the order reach the buyer (the seller ships it themselves, the platform holds stock, delivery services, collection in person, and for services — how is completion confirmed)?

Technical, geographic and practical constraints: is there anything to be known upfront (launch regions and languages, installable apps, payment services and the legal form of settlements, moderating content, a launch deadline, who will run the platform)?

saas.title: SaaS
saas.definition: Software people pay for again and again. The value is the work it does instead of the user; every user has an account, a plan and their own data.
examples: A bookkeeping or planning service
A tool for marketers, doctors or lawyers
A personal dashboard with calculations and reports
A team service with roles and permissions
signals: Money arrives repeatedly, not once
The user has an account and data of their own inside it
Your main risk is people not renewing, not people not buying
questions: What the product does and its main path: what exactly does a person or a company get from your service? Describe the main route — from the first sign-in to the moment the user gets the result they came for.

Audience and roles: who are your customers (private people, solo founders, small business, large companies) and who inside them uses the product — owners, managers, specialists? Describe each type: industry, size, job.
The problem and the pain: what key working task or pain do you close for this audience?
The core at launch: which capabilities must be in the first version, and which can wait? Describe what the product is meaningless without.
Pricing and monetisation: how is it paid for (a free tier, a flat subscription, per user, by usage, one-off purchases, enterprise terms)? Name the plans and what each includes.

Teams and organisations: how are accounts arranged (a personal account, a shared workspace with roles, several organisations under one person)? Who invites whom, who sees what, and what happens when an employee leaves?

Sign-in and security: how do people get in (email and password, signing in through other services, single sign-on for large customers, two-step confirmation)? Do your customers impose requirements on how data is protected?

Alternatives: how is this solved today, when neither your service nor a competitor's is there (spreadsheets, somebody else's product that does not quite fit, manual work, hiring a person, not at all)?
The ideal outcome: what is the perfect result for a customer — the one that makes them renew every month? At what moment do they realise the money is well spent?
Competitors: who are your direct and indirect competitors? Name the products and links, say what you like about them and what you find weak.
What sets you apart: the approach, the features, simplicity, price, speed of adoption, being built narrowly for one industry?

Limits and overdue payment: what happens when a user exceeds their plan or has not paid for the new period — access closes at once, the product drops to the free tier, a grace period with a warning? And what happens to their data meanwhile?
Taking money: which payment services and features are needed (recurring charges, invoices for companies, several currencies, taxes, refunds, changing plan mid-period)?

First experience and activation: how does a new user reach their first benefit (a step-by-step setup wizard, hints over the interface, ready templates and sample data, an empty screen with one button)? Within how many minutes should they see a result?
Open access and integrations: do customers need access to your API and outgoing event notifications? Which third-party systems must the product connect to first?

Metrics and the owner's workplace: what do you need to see about your own service (revenue and its growth, churn, customer lifetime, active users), and do you need a support console — find a customer, extend a subscription, sign in as them to investigate?
Interface style and complexity: what product do you want — as simple and fast as possible, or powerful and flexible with many settings? Are there interfaces worth taking as a model?

Technical and practical constraints: is there anything to be known upfront (a mobile version or app, where data is stored and what is required of it, the load you expect, a launch deadline, who will support the product after launch)?

crm.title: CRM system
crm.tagline: An internal system, not a website
crm.definition: A team's workplace: leads, deals, tasks and every conversation with a client in one place. It has no visitors — it has employees with different rights, and what matters most is not how the screen looks but how the records are shaped and by what rules a deal moves along the funnel.
examples: A sales team losing enquiries between messengers
An agency running client projects from enquiry to delivery
A clinic or service with bookings, calls and repeat visits
A company that outgrew a spreadsheet but does not want somebody else's CRM
signals: Enquiries arrive from several places and some of them are lost
The manager cannot see which stage each deal is standing at
Records live in spreadsheets, and every employee has their own copy
questions: The business and its processes: what field and what size of company is this system for? Which records are the central ones (leads, deals, clients, projects, enquiries, support tickets)?
Who works in the system: describe every role and type of user (sales people, team leads, marketing, support, administrators, outside contractors) and what each of them must be able to do.
The problem and the pain: what is the main problem the business is solving with this CRM (lost leads, no oversight of the sales team, chaos in tasks, a long deal cycle, weak analytics)?

The client cycle and funnels: what does the path look like from first contact to a closed deal and repeat sales? How many funnels are needed, what stages do they have, what happens at each, and by what rules does a deal move on?
Records and fields: which objects do you need (leads, contacts, companies, deals, products and services) and what fields, tags and flags must their cards carry?

Access rights: what are the rules of visibility — can a salesperson open somebody else's deal, are they allowed to export the database, who deletes records and reassigns owners? Do you need a hierarchy of managers and their teams?
Channels that create leads: which sources must automatically create a lead or a task (a form on the site, telephony, Telegram and WhatsApp, email, social networks, ad campaigns)?
Alternatives: how do people handle these tasks today (spreadsheets, paper notebooks, messengers, notes, somebody else's CRM that did not fit)?
The ideal outcome: what result of working in this system would leave both the manager and the team as productive and satisfied as possible?

Competitors and prior tools: which systems have you or your clients used before (amoCRM, Bitrix24, HubSpot, Salesforce, a Notion database)? What did not work, and which of their ideas are worth taking?
What must make your CRM fundamentally different from what exists (your own processes, simplicity, deep tailoring to your industry, automation, speed, price, integrations)?
Tasks and the calendar: how is task management arranged (tied to a deal or a client, deadlines, the type of task — call, meeting, email) and how are they viewed (a board, a list, a calendar)?
Modules and sections: what else must the system carry (emails and calls, documents and invoices, a knowledge base, internal team chat, a mobile app)?

Integrations with outside systems: what does the system exchange data with (accounting and stock, the website, email, ad accounts, payment services, other internal tools) and in which direction does the data flow?
Automation and triggers: what should happen without a human (assigning an owner, creating a follow-up task when the stage changes, an email or SMS to the client, a notification to the manager)?
Analytics and reporting: which summaries, charts and figures do you need (funnel conversion, average deal size, output per salesperson, how long a deal takes, lifetime value, reasons for losing)?
Import, export and migration: does an existing database need to be moved in, and in what form (spreadsheets, an export from the previous CRM)? Do you need reports and data exported out?
Interface and complexity: which system do you want — as simple and fast as possible, or flexible and powerful with many settings? Are there interfaces you like?

Technical, practical and legal constraints: is there anything to be known upfront (your own server or a cloud, how many users, requirements for protecting personal data, mobile apps, working offline, a launch deadline, who will administer the system)?

attestation.title: Certification and knowledge checks
attestation.tagline: Not knowledge, but a record an inspector will read
attestation.definition: A safety officer publishes the instructions, employees are examined on them, and the company gets a history: who, when, with what result. What separates it from an ordinary course is the cost of error — this record admits a person to dangerous work and defends the company at an inspection, so it must be neither lost nor rewritten after the fact.
examples: Occupational and fire safety on a production site
Clearance for equipment and work at height
Induction on hiring and after an incident
Checking contractors before they enter the site
signals: The result is needed not by the person but by an inspector
The certification expires, and the expiry matters
Failed means not admitted to work, and that must happen by itself
questions: A safety officer publishes instructions, employees sit an exam on them, and the company keeps a record of who has been trained. What main problem should this solve for you — and which of today's troubles do you want closed first (lost paper logs, no way to find quickly who passed, nobody watching the deadlines, preparing for an inspection takes weeks)?

Which knowledge checks come first (occupational safety, fire safety, electrical safety, clearance for equipment, professional standards, information security)? And which kinds of briefing do you need — induction on hiring, initial at the workplace, repeat on schedule, unscheduled after an incident or a new order, targeted for a one-off job?

Who is on each side: who creates the material and the questions (safety officers, department heads, HR, outside experts) and who sits the exam (everyone, particular roles, new hires, contractors and visitors)? How many people and how many departments?

The rules of sitting: how many questions in a paper, what score counts as a pass, is there a time limit, how many attempts? After how long is a retake allowed, and what happens after the last failed one — an in-person board, training again, suspension?

How is the matrix built — "role, workshop or department → the certifications they must hold"? Who maintains it, and what happens when someone moves to another role: which certifications are assigned automatically, which lapse?
Each certification has its own shelf life: one yearly, another every three years, a third only on hiring. How are those periods set, and how does the system know a particular person's is running out?

What exactly is saved for each sitting (who, when, which version of the instruction, which questions came up, what answers were given, how many attempts, who marked it, the board's membership)? Which of that is required by regulation and which is for your own peace of mind?

In what form does the source material arrive (documents and scans of regulations, editor files, training videos, slides, ready learning packages, plain instruction text)? How much of it is there and how often does it change?

A model can read an instruction and compose the questions itself — multiple choice, situational tasks such as "what do you do when a cable catches fire", checks on what is forbidden. Do you want that generation, and by what rule does it decide what in the instruction is important and what is secondary?

A question invented by a machine ends up in an official exam that admits a person to dangerous work. Should every generated question be reviewed by an engineer before it becomes active? Who answers for a wrong question — the one who approved it?

Which kinds of task are needed (one correct answer, several correct, putting actions in the right order, spotting a violation in a photo or diagram, an answer in the person's own words, a practical task marked by a human)?

Papers are drawn at random from a common bank — say twenty questions out of two hundred — so that people cannot pass answers to each other. Do you need that, and do you have enough questions for it to mean anything?

How many days ahead and through which channels should the employee and their manager be warned of expiry (email, a message, a notice in their account, a call to the manager)? How many reminders before the date, and what happens on the day it expires?

The date has passed and the person has not been certified. What should the system do: tell the manager, produce a suspension order, close access to equipment, disable the pass at the gate? How far may the system go on its own, and where must it only warn a human?
An unscheduled case: a new order comes out and everyone in one workshop must take a short check today. How is that assigned, and how quickly do people learn of it?

An instruction has been updated — the question that decides everything else. Do previous certifications become invalid and everyone is sent again, or only on a substantial change? Who decides what counts as substantial? Must the record hold which VERSION of the instruction the person was examined on?

On what do people sit the exam (a personal computer, a phone, a shared terminal at the gate or in the workshop)? Are there places with no connection at all — a building site, a remote facility — and do you need sitting offline with the answers sent later?

The legal weight of the record rests on it having been this person. How is identity confirmed at the start of an exam (an account, an access badge, a one-time code to the phone, face recognition)? Which of these will your inspectors accept?

Watching during the exam: should the system notice switching to another tab, forbid copying, photograph the person through the camera, spot a second person in frame? This is surveillance of living people at their workplace — where do you draw the line, and do employees know they are being watched?
Who marks written answers and practical tasks — an engineer by hand, or a model against a key? If a model, may it record a fail on its own, or is its opinion only advice to a human?
Do you need several languages and questions read aloud? For shop-floor staff and workers from abroad this decides whether they understood the question or guessed.
What confirms the result: is a mark in the system with a code sent to the phone enough, or do you need a qualified electronic signature from the employee? What will your inspectors accept?

What document comes out (a knowledge-check protocol on the prescribed form with a number, the board's membership and a verification code, a certificate, a statement)? Who signs it and where is it kept?

The record must survive an inspection three years from now, which means it cannot be altered after the fact — including by someone with access to the database. How is that ensured, and who must not be able to change a result at all?
How many years are results kept, and can they be exported for past periods? What happens to the records of someone who has left — deleted, anonymised, kept for the required term?

Do you need an inspector's mode — temporary access for an official to the history of one site over a given period, with no right to change anything? How is such access granted and how is it withdrawn?

Which roles are needed (author of the material, the one who assigns, the person examined, the department head, a board member, an administrator, an auditor) and what does each see? May a manager look at their subordinate's answers?

Which systems must be connected (HR records, single sign-on to the corporate network, document management, the permits system, the turnstiles at the gate)? Which way does the data flow — in, out, or both?

Which reports do management and inspections need (who passed and who did not, overdue by department, one person's history, the share trained per site, the most-failed questions, month-by-month movement)?

An employee does this once a year and does not remember how any of it works. What are your requirements for simplicity: in how many steps must they get from the notice to the exam, do they need feedback on their mistakes afterwards, and the ability to attach a scan of a signed paper acknowledgement?

scheduler.title: Scheduled automation
scheduler.tagline: A rule and a timer instead of judgement
scheduler.definition: A service that wakes itself at the appointed hour, goes where it was told, compares what it found against a condition and sends the result. There is nothing for it to decide: where judgement is needed you want an agent, here you want a rule. The product rests on three things invisible from outside — the schedule, the behaviour on failure, and the run log.
examples: Watching a price and reporting the moment it drops
Going through incoming mail and sending one digest a day
Collecting data from sites that offer no open access
A recurring report that assembles and sends itself
signals: Somebody checks the same thing by hand many times a day
The rule fits into one sentence: if this, then that
What matters is not missing the moment, not having a conversation
questions: Scenarios first: which recurring tasks are you covering (checking mail, watching prices and discounts, collecting data from sites, recurring reports, publishing, syncing data, calling someone else's API)? List the most important — those are where it starts.

Your audience: who creates and uses these automations? Describe every type — ordinary people, freelancers, marketers, analysts, small business owners, developers — and how willing each is to work out the settings.

The problem and the pain: what is the main thing the service solves (time lost to routine, the fear of missing a deal or an important email, the need to see how a price moves)? What is most irritating about doing it by hand?

How a person builds an automation: from ready templates, a visual builder, describing the task in plain language, code, or a combination? How manageable must it be for a newcomer on the very first evening?

Schedule and triggers: which ways of starting are needed (a fixed interval such as every 15 minutes, a cron expression, particular days and hours, a one-off delayed run, a manual run, an external event, a chain of several automations)?

Actions and where the result goes: what does the system do when it fires and where does the outcome land (a message in a messenger, an email, a row in a spreadsheet, a task in a tracker, a call to someone else's address, filling in a form)? Report every run, or only when there is news?

Data sources and integrations: what must the tool work with (email, sites with no open access, other people's APIs and incoming calls, news feeds, spreadsheets, databases, calendars, messengers, a CRM)? Which comes first?
Alternatives: how do people cope today, when your service is not there (checking manually every half hour, setting alarms, hiring an assistant, writing their own scripts, not at all)?
The ideal outcome: what result would leave a person fully satisfied (a message the very minute the price drops; one digest a day instead of a stream)?

Competitors and peers: what are you taking your bearings from (Zapier, Make, n8n, IFTTT, browser extensions, narrow price trackers, hand-written scripts)? What should be borrowed from how they work, and what do you find weak?
What sets you apart: simplicity, reliability, price, how deep the automations go, ready-made templates, working without code, speed, a narrow set of scenarios instead of everything at once?

Firing conditions: how is the rule "if this, then that" described (a price below a threshold, a word found in an email, a new entry appearing, a value changed since last time)? Do you need a condition builder by mouse, or is a simple form enough?

Reading sites and their defences: do you need to get past obstacles when collecting data (going through intermediate servers, a full browser instead of a plain request, dealing with "prove you are human" checks, signing in on the target site)? How lawful is that in your case?

Failures and retries: how does the system behave when something breaks — the target site is down, the network is gone, the answer came back empty? How many times to retry, at what interval, and when and whom to tell that a task is broken?
The run log: does a person need a detailed history of every task (success or failure, response time, what exactly came back, the saved response for debugging)? How long should it be kept?

Limits and payment: how are restrictions and money arranged (how many tasks may stay switched on, the minimum check interval on a free plan, paying per run or by subscription, what happens when a limit runs out)?
Technical and practical constraints: is there anything to be known upfront (hosting it yourself or in a cloud, running around the clock, the volume of data processed, languages, a launch deadline)?

ai-coach.title: AI coach and mentor
ai-coach.tagline: It leads a person, it does not hand out lessons
ai-coach.definition: A companion that remembers you between conversations: it sets goals, asks about them unprompted, and notices what you promised a week ago. What separates it from a course is that nothing is recorded in advance — the whole product is its character, its memory, and the point at which it stops and hands the person to real specialists.
examples: A habit tracker that asks first
A career mentor for those priced out of a human coach
A weekly goal review for a founder
A trainer guiding someone to an athletic target
signals: The value is in the conversation, not in pre-recorded material
Past sessions must be remembered, or everything starts from zero
People drop off without reminders, and the product must do the reminding
questions: Field and method: what area and what tasks does your coach work on (career, business, sport, habits, learning a skill, money, personal growth)? By what method does it lead — asking questions and never advising, giving direct recommendations, strictly tracking habits, playing a specific kind of expert?

Your audience: who will use the service? Describe every type of person in detail — age, occupation, level of experience, what hurts, what drives them — and how ready they are to work with an AI rather than a human.

The problem and the pain: what is the main thing the coach solves (a human mentor costs too much, discipline runs out, fear of looking foolish, decisions made alone, everything done in fits and starts)? What is stopping them most right now?

Character and voice: what should the coach be like — warm and supportive, strict and demanding, analytical, provoking, funny? What does it never do? Are there examples of speech worth taking as a model?

Memory and personalisation: what does the service remember about a person, and for how long (only the current conversation, past sessions, goals and failures, habits and preferences, key facts about their life or business)? Do you need entry tests, an assessment, a programme that adapts to the answers?

How the work runs: how is the interaction arranged (free conversation at any hour, scheduled sessions, short daily check-ins, a long programme with stages, homework and checking it)? How long is one session and the whole programme?

Limits of competence and handover: how must the system behave with topics outside its field — a person in crisis, health, legal and financial decisions? Where and how does it direct them, and at what point does it refuse to continue on its own?
Alternatives: how do people try to solve this today, when your service is not there (working with a human specialist, a journal, videos and books, talking to friends, nothing at all)?
The ideal outcome: what change must a person reach to call this their best helper? Describe where they are after a month and after a year.
Competitors and peers: what will you be compared with? Name the services, apps, bots and human-coaching platforms, with links. What do you like about them and what do you think is weak?
What sets you apart: depth of personalisation, the way it talks, the method, having a structure, combining with a real person, techniques of your own?
The form of conversation: in what form does it happen (text, voice messages, a call with a synthesised voice, going through documents and screenshots the person sends)?
Goals and progress: does the person need a screen with goals and achievements (a list of goals, a habit tracker, charts of mood and productivity, a weekly summary)?

Reaching out first: how does the coach start a conversation on its own (a reminder about a goal, a message saying "you promised to do this by Friday", a week in review, a reaction to several days of silence)? How often is it allowed to write first?
Key features: what else must be there (a library of materials, a community, handing over to a human specialist, a link to the calendar, data from wearables, exporting one's own records)?

Money and limits: how is it paid for (a subscription, per session or per programme, free access capped at so many messages a day, a trial, corporate plans)? What exactly is limited in the free version?

Technical and practical constraints: is there anything to be known upfront (how personal data is handled and stored, an installable app, languages, tuning to a specific user, the load you expect, a launch deadline)?

agents.title: Agentic automation
agents.tagline: The route is built as it goes
agents.definition: A system given one goal, which then decides for itself which steps will reach it: it walks through sources, reads what it finds, discards what contradicts, and assembles the rest into a document. What separates it from a schedule is that each step depends on the last — only the result is known in advance.
examples: A market study across dozens of sources, delivered as a report
A dossier on a company or a candidate before a meeting
An industry digest with the primary sources checked
A recurring study repeated month after month
signals: The task does not fit one query — it takes a dozen steps
What to look for next only becomes clear from what was already found
The output is a document with conclusions, not a row of data
questions: Tasks for the agent: which complex multi-step jobs must it handle (a market study, a dossier on a company or candidate, a legal check, gathering analytics, content research, running a process with branches)? Name the two or three you will start with.

Your audience: who sets the task and who reads the result? Describe every type — analysts, researchers, marketers, operations managers, business owners, developers — and how willing each is to check the agent's work.

The problem and the pain: what exactly do ordinary scripts and timed automations fail to cover? What eats a person's time today — walking through a dozen sources by hand, shallow analysis, missing what matters, the difficulty of pulling scattered findings into one document?

Stating the task and the plan: in what form does a person express the goal (a free sentence, a structured brief, a ready research template, a goal builder)? Does the agent draw up the plan itself, may it change the plan along the way, and does the person see that plan before it starts?
Tools and sources: what may the agent use (web search, reading pages, parsing PDFs, documents and spreadsheets, calling other APIs, running code, the company's internal databases and systems, email)?

How much it decides alone: what does the agent do unasked, and where must it stop and ask (collects data only · collects and recommends · acts with confirmation · acts on its own within set bounds)? What always needs confirmation — a paid call, sending something outward, writing into another system?

Citing primary sources: how is every claim in the final document backed (a footnote with the address, a saved quote or a snapshot of the page, the date it was collected)? What should be done with a claim that has no source?
Alternatives: how is this kind of research done today (searching and assembling a report by hand, hiring a freelancer or a consultant, buying a ready report, not at all)?

The ideal result and its form: what is the gold standard of an answer (a structured document with links to primary sources and charts, an interactive summary, filled-in tables with reasoning)? In what form should it arrive?

Competitors and peers: what are you taking your bearings from (AutoGPT, CrewAI, Devin, deep research in Perplexity, your own agent setups)? What attracts you in how they work, and what looks unnecessary?
What sets you apart — both from scheduled automation and from existing agent platforms (depth of reasoning, gathering step by step, adaptability, transparency of actions, human control)?
How the agents are arranged: one agent with a set of tools, or several with roles — planner, searcher, critic, writer? Can the owner change their roles and instructions?

Contradictions and gaps: what does the agent do when sources disagree (look for more, weigh how trustworthy each is, show the fork honestly in the report, refuse to conclude)? And what does it do when there simply is not enough data?
Depth and limits of one run: what bounds it (number of steps, number of pages read, spend on the model, total time)? What happens at the limit — does it stop dead or hand over what it managed?

Transparency of the run: does the person watch the steps live — what the agent is searching for now, what it is reading, what it is verifying? Is a full record of the run needed for review afterwards?

Memory between runs: should the results of past studies accumulate into a shared store of knowledge, so the agent does not search twice for the same thing? How is stale knowledge told apart from current?

Templates, failures and notifications: do you need ready scenarios for frequent studies? What happens when a step fails — retry, go around, stop? How does the person learn that the work is finished or broken?

Constraints and safety: is there anything to be known upfront (hosting it yourself or in a cloud, working with confidential data, what the agent must never do at all, mandatory human oversight, a launch deadline)?

competitors.title: Competitor intelligence
competitors.definition: A project that reads competitors' pages, social accounts and marketplaces by itself, stores what it finds and shows the movement: what changed, when and by how much. The platform's own browser does this without you walking the sites by hand.
examples: Watching prices and assortment
Monitoring a competitor's vacancies and hiring
Tracking their publications and advertising
Collecting and digesting reviews across the market
signals: You already check other people's sites by hand, just irregularly
Your decision — price, assortment, wording — depends on someone else's move
You need the history of changes, not a single snapshot
questions: The main goal and hypotheses: what does the service solve (comparing capabilities, finding pricing patterns, watching for new features, a financial benchmark, taking apart other people's sales funnels)? Which guess about the market do you want checked first?
Who uses the result: who reads the reports inside your system (you, a product person, a marketer, an analyst, the coding agent, other agents) and what decision does each of them make from it?

The list of competitors: who are we watching at launch — give the addresses. How many now, and how many might there be? Direct only, or indirect and potential too? How is the list extended — by hand, from a file, by searching the niche automatically? Which of them should the system be tested on first?

What exactly is collected: which data is extracted (prices and plans, the set of capabilities, the text and promises on pages, reviews, news and release notes, discounts, changes in public documentation, job openings, traces of the technology used)? Which of these is central and which incidental?

Depth of access: where does the needed data sit (public pages only · pages behind a sign-in · content behind a subscription · personal accounts · things that appear only after scripts run on the page)? How deep are you willing to go?
