Two modes: do you need both — a deep one-off study on request, and a light regular sweep? If so, how do they differ in depth, cost and frequency? On what schedule does the regular one run, and what else can trigger it besides time?

Kinds of comparison: which comparisons matter most (a has-it / has-it-not matrix of capabilities, prices and plan grids side by side, taking apart positioning and promises, benchmarking, a summary of strengths and weaknesses)?

How it was gathered before: how did you or your analysts get this until now (by hand into a spreadsheet, buying ready reports, subscribing to competitors' newsletters, not at all)? How long did it take?

The ideal outcome: what counts as flawless work (a summary report with charts of the month's changes, an instant message saying a competitor cut prices by twenty percent, your own data table answering your question)?

History and snapshots: do you need an archive of states, to see how a page or a competitor's pricing looked three months ago? What exactly accumulates over time (prices, capabilities appearing and disappearing, changes in wording, new pages, a rebuilt site structure) and for how long is it kept?

Accounts and paid access: do you need a vault of logins, sessions and sign-in files to reach closed parts? Who creates and pays for those accounts? What is done where a paid subscription or a card is required — accounts bought in advance, free trials only, or do we not go there at all?

Proxies and geography: do you need visits from different countries and cities — many competitors show different prices by region. Which regions matter, and should the exit address change between requests?

Browser fingerprint and behaviour: how often does the browser profile change — every request, every site, or does one competitor keep a steady profile of its own? Do you need imitation of a live person (cursor movement, pauses while typing, random scrolling, visits to unrelated pages)?

Defences and "prove you are human" checks: how does the system behave when it meets a check or a protection screen — back off and mark the page unavailable, try another way, call an outside recognition service? Where is the line you will not cross?

What the agent can do on someone else's site: which actions does it need (moving between sections, signing in, starting a trial subscription, downloading files, working inside a personal account, walking through pagination, waiting for content that appears late, taking screenshots)?

Evolving skills: a competitor rebuilt their markup — what happens? Does the agent rewrite the parsing itself and save the new map without a human, or stop and call for one? How independent is it overall, and where must it ask?

Transparency: do you need to see what the agent actually did on the site (a step-by-step log, screenshots at the moment of failure, a recording of the session, the network calls)? Is that for your trust, or for debugging?

Failures, blocks and bans: what happens when the site is down, the markup changed, the session expired, the page turned out to be paid, or the exit address was banned? How many retries, at what interval, switching to a backup channel, pausing for a day, telling the administrator?

Limits and concurrency: what bounds a single session (time per site, spend on the model, traffic volume) and how many competitors are processed at once? What happens at the limit — a hard stop or a partial result?

Storage and security: where do raw and processed data live (tables for numbers, a vector store for texts, file storage for page snapshots)? Who has access, how long are they kept, and how are they deleted on request?

Patterns: should the system find the recurring by itself — a pricing strategy, the rhythm of releases, reactions to market moves, the seasonality of discounts? Or does a human draw conclusions and the system only shows data?

A summary in words: do you need a short conclusion from the model on each report — "this week two of five raised B2B prices by fifteen percent"? How far can such a conclusion be trusted without checking the numbers, and must it point back at the rows it came from?

How it is shown: which forms of presentation are needed (comparison tables, charts of change over time, radar diagrams of capabilities, heat maps, before-and-after cards, a timeline of events, written reports)?

The structure of report pages: how is all of it grouped (a page per competitor, summary comparisons, a chronology by run date, a split by product category, an arbitrary slice over a period)? What does a person see first on opening the section?
Before and after: do you need a visual breakdown of differences, highlighting what appeared and what vanished on a competitor's page? At what level — the text, the block, the screenshot?
Working with a report: should tables and charts be live (sorting, filtering, search, hiding columns), and do you need exporting out — as a spreadsheet, a document, something printable?

Access to reports and to data: who opens them and how (a closed section behind a sign-in, a link with a password, a ready file by email)? Do you need programmatic access so your other services can collect the findings themselves?

Notifications and thresholds: what must be reported at once and where (a message in a messenger, an email, a call to your own service, a mark in the interface)? What is the threshold — any change, a price move beyond a few percent, a new capability appearing?

Manual correction: should an analyst be able to fix or extend what was collected — correct a misread price, add something the site does not state? How is machine-collected told apart from human-corrected in the report?

Legal and ethical bounds: what is categorically not to be done — by your decision and by law? What request rate do we hold so as not to disturb someone else's site; how do we treat terms of use, the site's own crawler instructions, personal data in reviews, and copyrighted text? Are there countries or platforms we do not touch at all?

company-brain.title: Company brain — engineering
company-brain.tagline: All the company's knowledge in one place
company-brain.definition: A project that gathers what the company knows — documents, correspondence, tasks, the code base, people and their roles — puts it into structure, keeps it in your own database and gives it back as reports and as answers that cite their source.
examples: A knowledge base that answers from your documents
A map of employees, roles and areas of responsibility
A digest of the code base and its changes
Regular reports for the head of the company
signals: Key knowledge lives in people's heads and in chats
A new employee takes weeks to get up to speed
The same question gets asked again and again
questions: The system builds a single understanding of the whole project from its repositories, so that anyone on a large team can get answers about structure, goals and connections without hunting down the one person who remembers. What is the main problem of your team that this should remove?

The value of such a system is measured by the questions it answers. Which questions must people be able to ask first — "how is the team organised", "what are that department's goals", "where is this feature implemented", "what interfaces exist for this", "who owns this piece", "how does the neighbours' work affect mine"? Which of the "I do not understand how this works, who owns it, or how it touches me" situations hurt most today, and should a new hire get their first tour of the architecture through this system?

Repositories will be the foundation: a map is built from each and lands in the vector store. Which repositories are in the compulsory circle at launch (a single store of all code or separate services, the front end, the back end, infrastructure, documentation, shared libraries) and where do they live — GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, your own server?

Depth of analysis decides what the system can answer at all: from descriptions it retells the intent, from code it tells how things actually are. How deeply should it understand a repository — only descriptions and documentation, also the folder structure and names, the whole code with comments, or all the way to the links between entry points, calls to databases and dependencies between services?

A map lives exactly until the next change to the code. How often is it refreshed — on every push to the main branch, when a merge request opens, once a day on a schedule, by hand, only when certain files change? What happens to the answers in the meantime, while the map lags behind?

The system's output is a conversation. Through which channels will people ask (a bot in a messenger, a chat inside the portal, a panel in the development environment, email), and which is the main one at launch? Do you need voice, so questions can be asked on the move?

Knowledge about a project is not always shared knowledge. Which roles and access levels are needed: everyone sees everything, a split by team and repository, some parts hidden entirely? Should a developer on one team see the internals of another team's services?

Not everything in a repository is equally valuable: some files describe the intent, the rest are its execution. Which files do you consider the primary source of truth about goals and structure (the description at the root, a separate architecture document, interface descriptions, build and deployment files, comments in the code, decisions written down as separate documents)?

A repository map is a structured distillation, read not by a human but by the search. Which entities and connections must it extract (modules and services, interfaces, databases and queues, the owning team, the purpose of a module, dependencies on other repositories, key business processes)?

Some repositories are private, and the system needs a way in. How is access granted (a service account with read-only rights, a developer's personal token, keys), who creates it, and what happens when access is revoked?

The change history answers questions no document contains: who wrote this, why it was decided this way, what was tried before. Should the system read the history of changes, the authors and the review discussions — and do you understand that in doing so it also learns about people?

To answer "how does that department's work affect mine", code is not enough: you need the organisational side — who owns what and what the units are aiming at. Where does the system take this from (the repositories themselves, separate documents, the company's staff structure, entered by hand, all together)?

Links of the kind "this service depends on that one, and that one belongs to that team" go stale faster than anything else. Should the system find and maintain them itself — from calls between services, shared databases, shared libraries, process descriptions — and how does it answer the direct question "which of other people's work touches my module"?

Text and code are turned into numeric representations, and the search runs over those: whether the right fragment is found at all depends on that choice. Which vector store do you prefer, and which model should build the representations — a hosted one or your own, running inside your perimeter?

A whole file is not put into the search — it is cut into pieces, and whether a found piece makes sense depends on how it was cut. How should it be cut: by logical units of code (a function, a class), by document headings, by an equal number of characters, differently for code and for text?

On top of meaning-based search one can build a graph of explicit links: this service calls that one, that one belongs to a team. Search finds the similar; a graph finds the exact. Do you need the graph, and which links must it hold?

Sooner or later the description and the code diverge: the document says one thing, the code another, and a third thing is described by nobody. What should the system do — trust the code, trust the document, show both and flag the discrepancy, refuse to answer? And what does it do when there is no information at all?

A separate layer could assemble a weekly summary of what each team has been doing, from their movement in the repositories. Do you need such a layer — and do you understand that it is a machine's summary of living people's work, which those people will read?

One question is rarely the whole of it: an answer is usually followed by a clarification. Should the system hold a long conversation, remembering what was said, and ask clarifying questions back — or is answering each request on its own enough?

A technical answer is worth as much as it can be verified and used at once. How thoroughly does the system answer about interfaces, data formats and ways to connect — a short conclusion, a link to the exact place in the code, a ready example request, a link to the specification? And what does the ideal answer to a hard question look like: a short conclusion, then the sources, a diagram, and a way to go deeper?

A product question — "what are that department's goals this quarter and how do they touch our database" — is not answered by code. Should the system assemble such an answer from documents itself, or honestly redirect to the person responsible? Which is worse: a plausible invention or a refusal?

Sometimes an explanation is easier drawn than described. Should the system produce diagrams right inside the answer — a map of links between services, a sequence of calls, a simplified architecture? In what form are they most useful to you?

One of the main scenarios sounds like this: "I need data from your service". How should the system answer — with a ready code example of the call, a link to the interface description, the contact of the responsible engineer, all of it at once?

The system can not only answer but also warn first: "the neighbouring team changed the sign-in interface, this may break your module in the next release". Do you need such messages, on which events, and to whom exactly do they go? What keeps them from becoming noise that people stop reading?

Besides code, a company knows a great deal about itself in other places. Which sources are worth connecting now or later (an internal document base, a task tracker, conversations in work chats, recorded architecture decisions, meeting notes, the staff structure)? Which of these matters most?

Part of the knowledge is written nowhere and lives only in someone's head. Do you need a way to add it by hand — a note on a module, a team's goal, a decision put on record? Who may do that, and how is what a human added told apart from what the machine collected?

Besides "how does this work", a large system raises the question "where will it crack". Should the system answer about accumulated technical debt, risks, bottlenecks and the dependencies whose failure stops everything else? Or are those conclusions a human must draw?

The quality of such a system is measured not by what it answered but by how right the answer turned out to be. Which measures matter to you (accuracy, completeness, speed, the share of questions that got any answer at all, people's own judgement)? Do you need "useful / useless" marks, a history of conversations, and a record of questions left unanswered?

The hypothesis behind this architecture is simple: repository maps plus meaning-based search will give a shared view of the project. Like any hypothesis, it will hold in some places and not in others. Which questions do you think it will answer well, and where will it be weak? Do you have repositories or parts of the project that fit this approach especially well or especially badly?

The system reads all of the company's code, and with it whatever ended up in that code by accident. Which safety rules do we lay down from the start: what must not be shown to certain roles, what to do with keys and passwords it finds, with production settings, with employees' personal data in the change history? Are there repositories the system must never touch?

business-brain.title: Company brain — business
business-brain.tagline: One answer instead of six tabs
business-brain.definition: It gathers into one place everything that turns around the customer: enquiries, correspondence, calls, deals, invoices, delivery and support tickets. Anyone asks in plain words and gets an answer that would otherwise take an hour across six systems. The price of that convenience is the company's entire commercial secrecy sitting in one place.
examples: "What is happening with this client and why did they ask for a discount"
A summary on a salesperson: conversion and reasons for losing
Three years of history with a supplier
A post-mortem: why the deal fell through and what preceded it
signals: Answering a simple question means opening several systems
What is known about a client lives in one salesperson's head
The manager learns of a problem once it has already happened
questions: The system brings sales, marketing, finance, delivery and support into one place, so that a question about a customer is answered not by a person with a good memory but by the company itself. What main pain of your team should this remove, and which of those areas must be in the very first version?

The value is measured by the questions it answers. Which should people ask first — "what is happening with this client", "what enquiries does this salesperson have", "why did this deal fall through", "what is the history with this supplier", "how much did we earn from them this year"? Which "I cannot quickly see what is going on" situations hurt most today?

The system's knowledge rests on a few central entities around which everything else gathers. Which are central for you — customers, deals and enquiries, salespeople, suppliers, goods and services, payments, support tickets, ad campaigns?

The same person writes from a personal mailbox, replies in a messenger and appears in the sales system under a different name. Until the system knows these are one client, there will be no complete answer. By what signs should records be joined into one person or company, and what happens in case of doubt — merge, or ask?

Enquiries arrive from several places at once, and a channel left out means a customer lost. Which channels must be connected (mailboxes, forms on the site, messengers, telephony with call recording, partner enquiries, marketplaces)?

The sales system is usually considered the main one, and is also the one that most often disagrees with reality. Which system must be connected, and what is its role: the single source of truth, one source among several, or may the system supplement and correct it with what it finds in correspondence and bank records? What else do we connect at the first stage?

Here, separating rights is not a convenience but a duty. May an ordinary salesperson ask the bot for the company's net profit or a colleague's salary? Which roles are needed and what does each see: their own clients, the whole team, the finances, anonymised statistics?

The result of that joining is a single card where everything about one client flows together. What do you mean by "exhaustive information": purchase history and sums, all correspondence and calls, support tickets, personal discounts and special arrangements, debts, salespeople's internal notes? Which of these is compulsory and which desirable?

Individual records mean little without the links between them. Should the system show which salespeople worked with a client, which suppliers stand behind which deals, which advertising brought this enquiry, and how one affected the other?

Money is the most checkable part of an answer and the most sensitive. Where do the financial figures come from (the accounting system, stock records, bank statements, payment services, expense spreadsheets) and who is responsible for their accuracy?
The path of money begins long before the deal — at an ad impression. Which advertising and analytics systems should be connected so the road from the ad to the revenue is visible?

A sale does not end at payment: after it come the warehouse, dispatch and delivery. Which stock systems and delivery services must be connected to answer about availability, timing and the status of a particular parcel?

After the sale comes support, and that is where the truth about the product shows. How should tickets, complaints and returns be collected, and how should the system answer "what three problems most often hit customers after buying this item, and how are they resolved"?

A relationship with a supplier is the same kind of history as with a customer, seen from the other side. What should accumulate (purchase price history, terms and deferrals, reliability and missed dates, delivery times) and which questions must it answer?
Contracts live for years, and usually one person remembers them. Do you need search across contract texts and tracking of dates — when one expires, when it renews itself, where the special terms are?

At first launch you must decide how far back to start: the past can be loaded, but that costs time and money. How much history do we raise — a year, three, everything there is, or do we start from a clean slate? And how deep per deal: only the current state, or the whole chronology of contacts with correspondence, calls and internal comments?

Most of what is known about a customer sits not in fields but in words: long conversations, call recordings, a salesperson's notes, scanned documents. What is done with these — keep them whole, shorten to the essence, extract only facts and entities, transcribe speech and read text on images? Should the mood of a conversation be detected?

An answer is only as good as the data is fresh. How often is it refreshed — immediately on an event (an email arrived, a deal changed status), every few minutes, hourly, on a schedule? Where is a delay acceptable and where is it not?

Some answers are numbers that must be calculated rather than found. Which figures must the system compute on request (customer lifetime value, cost of acquisition, average deal size, deal margin, debts, late payments, the sales funnel, sources of enquiries, delivery load)?

A separate class of questions is about people's work. How should the system answer "show this salesperson's conversion this month and the main reasons customers said no"? Who may see such answers, and does the employee know they are being asked about?

A salesperson's correspondence can be not only stored but checked against how the company expects people to speak. Do you need such checking against the rulebook with mistakes highlighted — and do you understand that this is oversight of people, not only of quality?

The most valuable answer is not "what happened" but "why". Should the system explain causes: why a deal was lost, why conversion fell, why delivery was late? How far can that explanation be trusted, and must it point back at the records it came from?

A break in the supply chain shows in the data before it shows in a complaint. Should the system flag bottlenecks itself — that delivery to this customer is late because of the carrier, that a supplier's dates keep slipping?

The system can write first, without waiting for a question: "a key client did not renew, though they always paid before the fifteenth", "this deal has stalled", "a harsh review came in". Do you need such messages, on which events, to whom exactly, and what keeps them from becoming noise?

Data from different systems will inevitably disagree: sales says paid, the bank shows nothing. What should the system do — trust one source, show both and flag the discrepancy, raise an alarm? Who resolves it?

The answer must arrive where the person works. Through what do we talk (a messenger bot for managers, a chat inside the portal, a panel right inside the sales system, email), and which is primary at launch?

Working through a difficult client rarely fits into one question. Should the assistant hold a long conversation, remembering what was said, and ask clarifying questions — or are pinpoint answers enough?

These data hold other people's personal details and commercial secrets. Which rules do we lay down at once: what to hide in answers (card numbers, documents, private phone numbers), how to meet data-protection law, how long to keep, how to delete on request, what to do when someone demands erasure?
Some answers are better shown than described. Should the system build charts, summary tables and exports right inside the answer — and in what form is it most convenient for you to take them?

No system knows what was never written down, and none is free of error. Do you need a way to add knowledge by hand — an important note on a client, an arrangement, a correction to a misread sum? And by what will you measure the brain's quality: speed of answer, completeness, the share of questions that got a useful answer, time saved on working things out?

custom.title: Your own direction
custom.definition: A direction for what is not in the list above. There are no ready questions here and there will not be: you write them. The twenty sets beside it cover what could be foreseen; this one exists precisely for what could not — dropping in "seven universal questions" would bring back the very trouble that choosing a direction was meant to end.
examples: A product unlike any of its neighbours
Your own industry, with its own words and rules
An internal tool for a single task
An idea that does not have a name yet
signals: None of the directions above describes what you are building
Ready-made questions would steer the conversation the wrong way
You know what you need to be asked better than we do

manyBody: This server does not carry one site. Today you describe your first product — a landing page, say; tomorrow a store appears on the same server, and next month a company brain that automates your internal work. Nothing new has to be bought or deployed for that.

Each product gets its own place: a public one lives at its own address, an internal one becomes a tab in your control panel, and an automation needs no screen at all — it works through channels and on a schedule.

That is why questions and use cases belong to a product rather than to the server. When the agent picks up a task, it knows which pages and which data are that product's — and does not touch the one next door.
projectPicker.manyHint: Nothing to choose here yet: your first product is created for you as soon as your use cases are written. You will add the second one from this page, on the day you need it.
projectPicker.lead: Choose the structure of your project
projectPicker.hint: Tap a direction — a description with examples and telling signs opens. Once you choose, you get seven questions written for that direction alone.
projectPicker.chosenHint: Below are the seven questions for this structure. Rewrite them, dictate them, delete them or add your own — then start the interview.
projectPicker.productsHint: Each product has its own use cases, its own pages and its own data. Pick one to work on it, or add the next.
projectPicker.addHint: A second product starts the same way as the first: its structure, its seven questions, its own use cases.
projectPicker.soonTitle: A second product is not ready yet
projectPicker.soonBody: The register already holds products and the agent already reads them, but creating a second one from this page arrives in the next batch. Until then this page belongs to your first product.
projectPicker.rootsHint: Derived from the record, never invented. The coding agent writes inside these and nowhere else — shared code goes to components/ and lib/.
projectPicker.devHint: Where this product stands in the work, and which development steps belong to it. Set by the agent as it goes; the numbers are the index it searches by.
projectPicker.pagesTitle: Planned pages against what is built
projectPicker.pagesHint: The plan comes from your use cases and you may edit it freely; what is built is counted from the folders every time this page opens, never stored.
projectPicker.pagesNoPlan: No plan yet — it appears together with your first use cases.
projectPicker.pagesExtra: Built but not in the plan
projectPicker.pagesExtraHint: Not a mistake: either the plan is behind, or these pages belong to something you have not described yet.
projectPicker.editNameHint: In English — it goes into reports, the page plan and your conversations with the agent. Renaming is safe: the product's paths hang on its permanent id, never on its name.
projectPicker.editDescHint: In your own language — only a human reads it. Up to 200 characters: what this product is and how it works, enough to tell it from your others at a glance.
projectPicker.noDescription: No description yet — it is written when the cases are analysed, or you can write it yourself.
projectPicker.delDanger: This is how a product's description dies. The cases are the answer to “what is being built and for whom”; without them the coding agent refuses to build, and restoring them means going through the whole interview again.
projectPicker.delGoes: Leaves the panel: the product record, its {n} use cases, the seed, the interview transcript and the page plan. They move to the archive inside your project — nothing is erased.
projectPicker.delStays: Stays on disk untouched: everything already built — its pages, its code in lib/products/, its database tables. Deleting the description does not delete the application.

useCases.gateMissing: No user cases yet — development does not start without them. Answer the questions below; the Quiz turns your answers into cases.
useCases.gateUnconfirmed: {confirmed} of {total} cases confirmed. The rest are still the model's guesses — read them and confirm, or correct them first.
useCases.gateReady: All {total} cases are confirmed. This is what the agent builds against.
useCases.flowDocTitle: How user cases are born — four stages
useCases.flowLead: User cases are the description of what your product must do, written before anything is built. They are not documentation about the product: they are the input your agent builds from. Four stages, and each one exists because the previous one alone is not enough.
useCases.flowStep1: You see the questions before answering any of them, and you own the list: rewrite one in your own words, dictate it, delete what does not apply to your product, add what is missing. A question written for someone else's product walks you through someone else's product — and that only becomes visible at the end, when everything has to be redone.
useCases.flowStep1Out: A list of questions that fits your product, saved with the project.
useCases.flowStep2: You answer one question at a time, in writing or by voice. These answers become the SEED: every later request to the model starts from them. This is where the direction of everything that follows is set — not the wording of it, the direction.
useCases.flowStep2Out: A seed the model reads on every call afterwards.
useCases.flowStep3: The model turns your seed into questions of its own, one at a time, going deeper where you were brief. When answering gets tiring, the auto-quiz asks five NEW questions and answers them for you, out loud, so you can read and correct instead of composing. An answer it had to guess starts with the word "Assumption" — an unmarked guess would become a fact nobody chose.
useCases.flowStep3Out: A conversation broad enough to decompose into separate scenarios.
useCases.flowStep4: Finishing the interview turns the conversation into numbered cases — and every one of them is orange, because a case written by a model is still a proposal. You read each one and confirm it, correct it in your own words, ask the model to rewrite it after your remark, or delete it. Any edit turns the case orange again: green must mean "I agree with THIS text", not "I looked at it once".
useCases.flowStep4Out: Green cases — the ones development is allowed to start from.
useCases.flowQualityTitle: Rushed answers cost more than they save.
useCases.flowQuality: The model cannot invent what you did not say — from empty answers it produces empty cases, and the whole build stands on them. If the interview went badly, do not patch it: press “Start over”, and the questions, the seed, the conversation and the cases are cleared so you can do it properly. Nothing is destroyed — the old files move into an archive folder inside your project.
useCases.flowBoundaryTitle: Cases are the boundary of what gets built.
useCases.flowBoundary: Your agent builds what the cases describe and does not invent what they do not. That is the point of the gate: a skeleton agreed by you first, and only then millions of lines hung on it.
useCases.flowAfterTitle: The product keeps growing — so do the cases.
useCases.flowAfter: Later you simply add a case and tell your agent: “I added this case.” It becomes new development steps. Nothing has to be re-interviewed, and the earlier cases stay as they were.
useCases.flowWhere: In your project, as files: the cases in USE-CASES/CASES/, the raw material — every question and answer — in USE-CASES/RAW/. They travel with your repository, so the description of the product belongs to you, not to this panel.
useCases.flowAllDone: All four stages are done: every case is confirmed, and development can start from them. From here you only add cases as the product grows.
useCases.setupLead: These are the questions you will be asked. Read them before answering — a question aimed at someone else's product will walk you through someone else's product.
useCases.setupHint: Rewrite any of them in your own words, dictate them, delete what does not fit, add what is missing. The list is saved with your project, so your agent can see what you were asked.
useCases.setupSkip: Or you can start right away — press “Start the interview”.
useCases.setupMore: I agree to a fuller interview
useCases.setupMoreHint: These seven are enough to start. There are {n} more questions behind them — they go into the details, and the more of them you answer, the more precise the use cases will be.
useCases.setupFewer: I would rather answer only {n} questions
useCases.nextStepCreated: Confirmed. Development step № {n} has been opened — the queue starts from it.
nextSteps: Press «Push» in the footer — your project goes to your GitHub repository.
Open Env Variables and download .env.local — it carries the address of your data and the key.
On your own machine: git clone (first time) or git pull, then put .env.local in the project root.
Open Claude Code — or another coding agent — in that folder.
When it is done: git push on your machine, then «Pull» and «Deploy» here.
useCases.nextSayTitle: What to say to the agent
useCases.nextCopied: Copied — paste it to the agent.
useCases.resetBody: The intro answers and everything the Quiz produced from them will be cleared, and you will begin with a blank interview.
useCases.resetCounts: This clears: {answers} intro answers, {turns} conversation messages, {cases} cases ({confirmed} of them confirmed).
useCases.resetSafeDev: Your application is not touched. Cases describe the intent, not the code — whatever is already built keeps working exactly as it does now.
useCases.resetArchive: Nothing is destroyed: the files move to USE-CASES/RAW/ARCHIVE/ inside your project, so a mistaken reset can be recovered.
useCases.resetDone: Cleared — the interview starts from the questions
useCases.introLead: Seven questions to begin with. They are the seed: everything the Quiz asks and writes later grows out of your answers, so speak as freely here as you can — dictating usually gives more than typing.
introQuestions: What is this product, in one or two sentences? Say it as you would to a friend, not as a pitch.
Who is it for? Name one real person and the situation they are in — not a segment.
What brings that person to your product? The moment, the problem, the thing that made them look.
What do they do here, step by step, in the simplest case? Walk through it out loud.
What must be true when they are done — how do they know it worked?
What must NOT happen? Name the outcome you would call a failure even if everything else worked.
What already exists around this — a system, a team, a habit, a tool — that the product has to fit into?
useCases.introPlaceholder: Answer in your own words — voice works.
useCases.introSaved: Saved — the Quiz can start now
useCases.introTooShort: The answers are still too short to build on. A few sentences turn into far better cases than a few words.
useCases.voiceHint: Dictating usually produces a fuller answer than typing.
useCases.quizStartHint: The model asks one question at a time and turns the conversation into cases.
useCases.quizMoreHint: New cases are added to the ones below; nothing is overwritten.
useCases.quizPlaceholder: Answer in your own words — voice works.
useCases.quizHint: When the scenarios are clear, press «Create the cases» — the conversation is turned into numbered cases, each waiting for your confirmation.
useCases.modelBanner: Planning is where the model's strength shows most. The Quiz uses the model configured in the OpenAI section — a stronger one gives noticeably better cases.
useCases.autoPaused: Read the round, correct anything that is wrong, then keep it.
useCases.create: Finish the survey and generate the cases
useCases.ready: The model has enough — press «Create the cases».
useCases.added: {n} cases added — each waiting for your confirmation.
useCases.savedCase: Case saved — it went back to unconfirmed, read it once more
useCases.remarkTitle: Or say what is wrong with it — the model rewrites the case
useCases.remarkPlaceholder: e.g. it is not the manager who does this, it is the client — and there is no email
useCases.noKey: The Quiz needs an OpenAI key — add it in the OpenAI section, then come back.
useCases.noSeed: Answer at least one question in your own words first. The auto-quiz DEEPENS what you said — from a blank start it would invent a product you never asked for.
useCases.errKeyRejected: OpenAI refused the key — it is invalid, revoked, or belongs to a different account. Paste a fresh key in the OpenAI section.
useCases.errQuota: The OpenAI key works, but the account has no credit left. Top it up in your OpenAI billing, then try again.
useCases.errRateLimit: OpenAI is rate-limiting this key — too many requests in a short time. Wait a minute and try again.
useCases.errModelMissing: This key has no access to the selected model. Choose a model the account can use, or use a key that has it.
useCases.errUpstream: OpenAI could not be reached or answered with an error
useCases.errNoCases: The conversation holds nothing to turn into cases yet. Answer a couple of questions, or press the auto-quiz — then finish.
useCases.errSaveFailed: The cases were written but could not be saved on the server
useCases.legacyHint: This project has an older single USE-CASES.md. Move it into the folder — it becomes the first case, and the original file stays where it is.
useCases.legacyDone: Moved — check it among the cases
useCases.helpWhyTitle: Why nothing is built without this.
useCases.helpWhy: An agent that knows HOW to build but not WHAT FOR builds carefully and builds the wrong thing — and careful wrong work costs more than no work, because it also has to be removed.
useCases.helpRaw: Every question and every answer is written to USE-CASES/RAW/. The agent does not read it in normal work — it exists for the day you look for an idea that got lost when the cases were written.
useCases.helpConfirm: A case written by the model is a guess until a human reads it. Editing a confirmed case returns it to unconfirmed on purpose: confirmation must mean «I agree with this text», not «I looked at it once».
useCases.helpModel: The Quiz uses the model configured for this server:
useCases.autoAssumption: Answers beginning with «Assumption» are the model's guesses, not your words — correct them here, before they turn into cases.
useCases.autoAccepted: {n} question-answer pairs added to the conversation

passport.why: It is the only document that carries PROGRESS. The cases do not know the state of a screen, and the architecture does not know what is finished. Fold it into either and one of them starts being rewritten after every step.
passport.planesTitle: Entity is what the product is ABOUT, not a screen.
passport.planes: «Orders» is one entity even with a list, a card and a form. Splitting by screen inflates the table until it stops being a map. Sign-in, settings and legal pages do not belong here — they come with the platform.
passport.switchWhere: The first development step decides the type of the application and lays out the whole skeleton at once — every entity as an empty page, connected by navigation, at most ten of them. Each step after that moves one row.
passport.createdDoc: Document created — it is now a file in your repository
passport.createHint: This project has no PASSPORT.md yet. Create it from the template.

caseToStep.what: The passage from a confirmed use case to a queue of development steps: who starts it, how a step is named, and who may confirm what.
caseToStep.whySkillTitle: Why a skill, not an instruction.
caseToStep.whySkill: The main instruction is loaded in full at every session start, whether or not one line of it is relevant. A skill is delivered when a request calls for it. This document is a readable duplicate — when the two disagree, the skill is what actually runs.
caseToStep.switchWhere: The toggle is in Instruction set. Off means the agent does not run this flow and does not ask for it; the tools stay in place.

contentEngine.why: A post is three jobs at once: hold the data, render as a fully static page, and appear in the list. Done naively they are wired through a central registry that every author edits and every agent must load. Here there is none: one post is one folder, and the list is generated from the file system at build time.
contentEngine.shape: page.tsx — three lines of re-export · _components/index.tsx — the view · _data/{meta,en,ru,index}.ts — the data. Delete the folder and the post is gone everywhere; drop a folder in and it appears.
contentEngine.size: External links are always absolute, and third-party domains get nofollow. The only relative form allowed is the internal link home — [%SITE%](/ru) — whose label is replaced by your site name in that language. Every language cell of every post carries one, so an article gives weight away and receives some back.
contentEngine.switchWhere: npm run check:content rejects a relative link, a missing media file, a site name written into data, a declared language cell with no file, and a post with no translation. Each rule is a defect that already shipped once.
contentEngine.createdDoc: Document created — it is now a file in your repository
contentEngine.createHint: This project has no CONTENT-ENGINE.md yet. Create it from the template.

dynamicWorkflows.why: Not "many agents at once" — that is a fan-out. A dynamic workflow is a script Claude writes and a runtime executes: the script holds the loop, the branching and the intermediate results, so only the final answer reaches the conversation. Boris Cherny, who built Claude Code, calls it "an algebra for agents". Trigger it by saying "use a workflow"; /workflows shows every phase, its agent count and its token total while it runs.
dynamicWorkflows.cost: Every agent carries its own context and pays for it separately, and runs count against your plan's limits like any other session. Availability is not the question — workflows work on every paid plan, and on Pro you switch them on in the Dynamic workflows row of /config. Affordability is: if an ordinary session already reaches your limit before the work is done, a workflow will not fit. Price a big job by running one directory first; /workflows shows token use live and stops the run; a Large workflow warning appears past 25 agents or 1.5M projected tokens; the size guideline in /config aims Claude at fewer. Stopping mid-run is expensive — on resume every agent that started after the first unfinished one runs again.
dynamicWorkflows.gate: A workflow is an amplifier, and an amplifier pointed at a guess produces a large, tidy, expensive wrong thing. A hundred agents building carefully in the wrong direction is the most costly outcome available in this product. Cases are what point it, and the panel keeps this document locked until they exist and you have confirmed them.
dynamicWorkflows.guard: A wave is justified only where each unit's result is checked by a machine without you — translations, content sweeps, mechanical migrations, all of which already have guards here. Architecture, the client/server boundary, debugging a build: no. There, proving the answer costs more than producing it.
dynamicWorkflows.switchWhere: Do it after the campaign that justified it. Left on, every large request carries the question "should this fan out?", and for most work here the answer is no.
dynamicWorkflows.lockedTitle: Locked until your cases are ready.
dynamicWorkflows.lockedMissing: No user cases exist yet. Open the Use cases section — its Quiz turns a conversation into them.
dynamicWorkflows.lockedUnconfirmed: Cases exist but some are still unconfirmed. A case the owner has not confirmed is a guess the model wrote.
dynamicWorkflows.lockedReady: Cases are confirmed — this document can be switched on.
dynamicWorkflows.createdDoc: Document created — it is now a file in your repository
dynamicWorkflows.createHint: This project has no DYNAMIC-WORKFLOWS.md yet. Create it from the template.
dynamicWorkflows.whereTitle: Where it runs — nothing touches your production server.
dynamicWorkflows.where: No virtual machine is created anywhere. The runtime executes the script in isolation, and that isolation means the script itself has no filesystem or shell access — it only coordinates. The agents run inside your existing Claude Code session, on the machine running it, with the same permission mode, allowlist and sandboxing as any tool call you already make. Your operating system is irrelevant; nothing extra is installed. So they touch exactly what your session already touches — only up to sixteen at a time. Two consequences: subagents always edit files in acceptEdits mode whatever your mode is, and a running workflow takes no input, so stage sign-off means separate workflows.

topMenu.why: The navigation buttons of your application on :3000 — which pages they point at, in what order, and which of them collapse into a dropdown group. A button here is a page of your site, and only public pages are offered: a button leading somewhere the visitor cannot enter is a promise the interface will not keep.
topMenu.live: Saving writes the setting to the app's config on the server and immediately clears the cache of the page shell that holds the menu. The next page load shows it. Your pages stay static — nothing here makes them dynamic, and no deployment happens.
topMenu.empty: No buttons yet. The menu bar will still appear, with your logo and nothing else — that is a valid state, not an error.
topMenu.dragHint: Drag a page from the left to put it here; drop it between two buttons to choose its place. Drag a button to reorder. The arrow makes it a child of the button above, turning that one into a dropdown group.
topMenu.savedNow: Saved — already live on the site
topMenu.savedLater: Saved. The site could not be refreshed just now, so it will appear within ten minutes.
topMenu.authSide: Account drawer slides in from the
topMenu.baseLang: Base language — the value itself, not a translation
topMenu.langHint: You are editing translations. The base value stays as it is; an empty field means no translation, and the site falls back to the base.
topMenu.folderOnly: A folder — it groups pages but has none of its own, so it cannot become a button
topMenu.labelLimit: A menu label is at most 12 characters — longer ones are cut with an ellipsis on the site
topMenu.translateOne: Translate this label into every language of the app
topMenu.trDone: Translated — check the language tabs, then save
topMenu.trFailed: Translation failed. Try again in a moment.
topMenu.trNoKey: No OpenAI key on this server, so translation is unavailable. Add one in the OpenAI section.
topMenu.hideDialogTitle: Hide this page from the menu?
topMenu.hideDialogBody: The link disappears from the menu, and the page itself stays in your project — its files are not touched and its address keeps answering. You can put it back at any time by dragging it from the left column. To remove the page from the project, use Delete page instead.
topMenu.deleteDialogTitle: Delete this page from the project?
topMenu.deleteDialogBody: This removes the page's own folder and the three places that register it — the machine-readable surfaces, the sitemap and the starter's default footer. The address stops existing. This is a change to your project's files, not a setting, and the panel cannot undo it: restore it from your repository.
topMenu.deleteRebuild: Pages are served from the built output, so the deleted address keeps answering until the next build.
topMenu.deleteDone: Page deleted — rebuild to stop serving the old address.
topMenu.deleteFailed: Could not delete the page. Nothing was changed.

footerPages.why: The links at the bottom of your application on :3000 — which pages they point at, in what order, and what each is called. Only pages inside the footer-pages group are offered: the footer carries site pages, not the whole catalogue.
footerPages.contentTitle: Where the text of a page lives.
footerPages.content: Inside the project, next to the page — the same way a blog post works. Five pages ship as a worked example with placeholder text; a sixth is made by copying any of them. The pages are fully static and indexable: they carry a title, a description and structured data, like an article.
footerPages.empty: No links yet. The footer still renders — this is a valid state, not an error.
footerPages.buildTitle: A new footer page is built by the agent
footerPages.buildBody: This section arranges the links; it cannot create a page, and deliberately so — page text lives in the project, next to the page. Open the project on your own machine and tell the agent what you want to build: it has the skill for it. Send the project to GitHub, download .env.local so your copy reads this server's live data, then clone or pull and open the folder in Claude Code — or any coding agent.

cookieBanner.why: It decides whether visitors of your application see the consent strip at the bottom of the page. A private tool that stores no analytics has no use for consent — switch it off and the strip disappears, along with the Cookie settings button in the footer that re-opens it.
cookieBanner.words: The banner ships in all 82 languages, so it speaks whichever language a visitor arrives in. Consent written in a language somebody cannot read is not consent at all, which is why this is not left to be filled in later.
cookieBanner.page: The banner links to /<language>/cookies — an ordinary static page of your project. Its text is edited in the code beside the page, like a blog post; ask your agent for the manage-cookie-banner skill.
cookieBanner.on: Visitors are asked for consent, and can change their answer from the footer.
cookieBanner.off: No consent strip and no footer button. Choose this for a private tool with no analytics.
cookieBanner.saved: Saved — applies on the next page load, no rebuild

visibility.intro: Everything on this page is already built and holding. It is here so you can see what your project does without you — and check any of it yourself.
visibility.searchBody: Multilingualism with modern search optimisation and an installable app is normally a long development cycle — and the one AI-written projects lose quietly: pages drift from prepared to recomputed, translations start reading as copies of each other, and half the languages never reach search results.
visibility.searchSignals: The language signals are in place on every public page: each one declares itself the original, names its translations for every language you enable, and adds x-default for visitors you do not cover. Without them a search engine reads translations as copies of one another and whole languages never reach results — the site meanwhile looks perfectly fine.
visibility.modelsBody: The same is true for the reader people remember last and who is already arriving: the model. It comes itself, reads, and retells your site in its own words — so the project publishes a machine map of itself and a clean markdown twin of every page, built from the same text, so the two can never drift.
visibility.appBody: Your site installs like an app: its own icon on the home screen, a launch without browser chrome, and pages already seen opening without a network. The offline copy never replaces the live site — pages always come from the network while it is there, so a text you change in the panel appears immediately.
visibility.mapsBody: Robots are answered by name — search crawlers and models separately — and every map is declared to them in the first file they open. The map lists your home page, catalogue, blog and each article in every enabled language; it never lists pages behind a login, which exist per visitor and would return a sign-in form to a crawler.
visibility.noJsBody: Pages arrive as finished HTML from the server, and links are ordinary links — so the site reads and navigates with scripts disabled. This is not an advantage over a dynamic application, and interactive parts do degrade; but if yours is an informational site, visitors can use it safely in any environment, including ones where scripts are blocked for them.
visibility.cost: Here it is built, tested many times over, and it holds under load at no extra server cost: a prepared page costs the same at a hundred visits and at a hundred thousand.
visibility.choice: So the only thing left for you is the choice of languages. Whichever you pick, nothing else here is left to build.
visibility.docSeoTitle: Search optimisation: what is already built
visibility.docAioTitle: AI optimisation: what is already built
visibility.docPwaTitle: Progressive web app: what is already built
visibility.docRobotsTitle: Rules for robots: what is already built
visibility.offlineHint: Pages the visitor has already opened work without a network. Turning this off does not merely stop installing it — it removes the worker from devices that already have it and clears its caches.
visibility.imagesBody: The page arrives with the picture already INSIDE it: a tiny blurred copy of the image, about 150 bytes, is written into the markup — no separate request for it, so the visitor sees the shape and colours of the coming image in the same millisecond as the heading. Its space is reserved in advance, from its real dimensions, so the text does not jump when the file lands. The real image follows and replaces the blurred one by itself.
visibility.imagesSpeed: This is not decoration but two of the three figures a search engine measures your page by: the layout jump as things load, and how fast the largest element on screen appears — most often that element is an image. Meanwhile a phone does not download a file made for a large monitor: the needed sizes are produced from one original on demand, the format is matched to the browser, and everything below the first screen loads only when the visitor reaches it. Works with JavaScript disabled.
visibility.coverAlt: Lighthouse report: one hundred out of one hundred for performance, accessibility, best practices and SEO — beside this project catalogue
visibility.coverCaption: A real measurement of this project, not a marketing picture: 100 out of 100 across all four sections. On the left, the catalogue whose images came from the store.
visibility.dataBody: The project already has four stores, all on your server: rows, files, vector memory for search by meaning, and a knowledge graph for questions about connections. None of them needs to be started, configured or registered anywhere. You never design a schema: a new table is declared in one place and appears in every environment by itself — no migration files, no state where the server is ahead of your laptop.
visibility.dataCost: There is no step where free becomes paid and then becomes per-request-and-per-gigabyte. Data costs exactly what your server costs, however many queries it serves; a traffic spike turns into load on a processor you already paid for, not into an invoice. Outgrow it and you take a bigger server: the price rises linearly and the data travels with you, because it is files. And we spend that server carefully — public pages are prepared ahead and never query the database, answers are cached with a stated lifetime, a list is one query per page rather than one per row.
visibility.docDbTitle: The database: what is already built
visibility.docStorageTitle: Object storage: what is already built
visibility.docVectorsTitle: Vector memory: what is already built
visibility.docRagTitle: Agentic RAG: what is already built
visibility.authBody: Sign-in, accounts and access control work from the first minute and cost nothing: no cloud sign-in service to connect, no monthly fee per active user. Email and password work with no configuration; magic-link and Google sign-in are enabled by entering keys in the panel — the code is written. The library everything is built on supports over eighty providers: connecting one is an edit to a single file, by you or with our help.
visibility.authRoles: The most valuable part here is the least visible: roles are already attached to routes. To make a page available only to the right people you do not protect it — you build it on an existing route, and access lands with the holders of that role by itself. Four layers: personal account, staff, finance, administration; the first person to register receives every role at once. None of this costs speed: public pages are prepared ahead and never ask about sign-in.
visibility.designSystemBody: Nobody decides to make a site inconsistent — the drift accumulates one harmless edit at a time. A heading slightly larger here, a margin slightly tighter there, a card with a rounder corner on the third page. Each decision is reasonable on its own, and none of them looks like a mistake.
visibility.designSystemDrift: Then comes the part that matters for AI-assisted work: an agent reads the existing code as its example. While there is one way to describe a heading, it repeats that way. Once there are three, the agent draws a conclusion that is flawless from where it stands — there is no single rule here, so anything goes — and every new page adds a fourth. The more you build, the faster the drift. Here it is closed by primitives, tokens and four machine-checked laws that run inside the build: a violation does not reach the product, it stops the release.
visibility.docDesignSystemTitle: Design system: why the project does not drift apart
visibility.staticBody: Public pages are built ahead of time and served as files — with practically no load on the server. A dynamic page is recomputed on every visit: a multilingual site with a hundred pages and ten languages recalculates a thousand variants for every visitor, and growth in traffic turns into growth in the bill.
visibility.staticDrift: Static is much harder to build than dynamic, and the difficulty runs one way: any shortcut leads from static to dynamic, never back. Reading a cookie, a request header or a session check inside a layout turns the whole subtree dynamic — silently, without an error. A particular trap waits when private pages are added: since a dynamic layer now exists anyway, it feels simpler to make everything dynamic. Bills in the tens of thousands of dollars have grown from exactly a few such lines.
visibility.staticGuard: So the rule is held by a machine, not by an agreement. Public and private pages live in physically separate layers, and a check walks the entire public layer looking for signs of dynamics — on a match the build stops. Not a warning, not a log entry: the release does not happen until the violation is gone. A checklist is followed for as long as it is remembered; the first shortcut would bring dynamics back, and you would learn about it from the bill.
visibility.docStaticTitle: Static generation: the decision that costs the most

devTools.intro: These are the tools the project is BUILT with, not the ones that ship inside the product. They live on the developer's machine and never reach your visitor. The Tools section is about something else: ready-made pieces you can take into the application.
devTools.growing: The list will grow. Only what genuinely solves a task and has been proven in real work belongs here — not everything that can be installed.
devTools.browserBody: The Claude extension for Chrome gives the coding agent eyes: it opens a page in your browser and looks at the result of its own work. A whole class of defects cannot be found any other way — console errors, behaviour with scripts disabled, the service worker and offline, the page AFTER the code has run. In this project that is how nine errors on every page were found, and somebody else's error message standing in place of a video.
devTools.browserLimits: The boundaries are stated plainly: the agent never enters keys, passwords or payment details, never creates accounts or signs in to yours, never pays or accepts terms. So «make me an OAuth client in the Google console» or «set up Stripe» will not be done — that is your hand. It will walk you to the right screen, explain the fields, and verify the result after you enter it.
devTools.browserDoc: What it gives and what it does not
devTools.browserDocTitle: A browser for the agent: what it gives and what it does not
devTools.plannedNote: Candidates are discussed, but they enter this list only after solving a real task in a real project. Promising a tool that is not here yet means selling something that does not exist.
devTools.orderNote: The order is deliberate: first the tool you can do without, last the one you cannot. Install them in this order and mark each one when it is done.
devTools.codeTitle: Claude Code — the agent that writes the code
devTools.codeBody: This panel configures the project; Claude Code is what actually builds it. It runs in the terminal on your machine, reads your repository, writes and changes files, and can work inside your editor as an extension. Without it you have settings and nobody to act on them.
devTools.codeLimits: It runs on YOUR machine, not on this server. It works with the copy of the project you pull to your computer, and its usage is billed to your Anthropic account — this panel neither pays for it nor sees it.
devTools.editorTitle: Visual Studio Code — where you see the project
devTools.editorBody: A free editor for your machine. It is where you see the project as a whole — every file, every change, the difference before and after — and where Claude Code can live as an extension instead of a separate terminal window. This is the tool you cannot do without: without it the project stays a black box you can only ask about.
devTools.editorLimits: Any editor you already use will do — the panel does not check which one. The mark below says “I have an editor”, not “I have this exact program”.
devTools.editorInstall: Open the Visual Studio Code page
devTools.checkLabel: I have installed this — do not warn me about it
devTools.checkDone: Marked as installed — the warning is gone
devTools.checkUndone: Mark removed — the warning is back
devTools.helpAction: I need help with these tools
devTools.helpHint: Names not telling you much? Ask the developer — a short call is usually faster than an evening of reading.
devTools.helpBody: Your request goes to the developer at admin@fractera.ai. They will reply with times for a call and walk you through installing and using these tools in your own project.
devTools.helpFree: A free consultation is among the options — asking costs you nothing.
devTools.helpSentTo: Sent. The developer will reply to {email} with times for a call.
devTools.helpNotSent: The request could not be sent from this server. Copy the letter below and send it to admin@fractera.ai yourself — it will reach the same place.
devTools.helpEmailAsk: Enter the address to reply to
devTools.helpMailBody:
The user requests a consultation on activating and using the development tools in their project.

Page: {page}

designFonts.intro: Three roles, one decision each: headings, body text, and monospace. The set opens on the system font — it downloads nothing and reaches no third party.

heading.label: Headings
heading.description: H1 through H4. This is where a project gets its character.

body.label: Body text
body.description: Paragraphs, lists, captions — most of what a person actually reads.

designFonts.systemNote: Takes whatever the device already has. Nothing is downloaded, nothing leaves the page, and text is visible in the very first frame.
designFonts.previewText: The quick brown fox — Съешь ещё этих мягких булок 0123
designFonts.helpLabel: About fonts: where they come from and how they are connected
designFonts.helpWhere: The families in this list come from Google Fonts (fonts.google.com), all under a free licence — OFL or Apache. The files themselves are NOT stored on your server: a visitor receives them from fonts.googleapis.com, whose cache is already warm on nearly every device.
designFonts.helpHow: Saving writes the family name and its stylesheet URL into DESIGN-CONFIG/design-config.json on your server. The application reads that file on every render and emits two things: a <link> to the stylesheet in <head>, and a CSS variable that the type primitive uses. A <link> rather than an @import on purpose — the browser sees a link immediately, while an @import inside <style> costs an extra network round-trip before the font is even requested. No rebuild is needed; the change shows on the next page load.
designFonts.helpPrivacy: Connecting an external font hands the visitor IP address to Google servers. A German court has ruled that this alone breaches GDPR (LG München I, 3 O 17493/20). The system option avoids the question entirely: it never reaches outside. If you need both a custom font and that guarantee, the font files have to be hosted on your own server — that is a separate step, not a setting.
designFonts.helpAlphabet: A font without Cyrillic turns a Russian page into a row of rectangles, and the build will not warn you — the page renders perfectly, it is simply unreadable. Every entry states which alphabets it covers; check it against the languages you switched on.
designFonts.helpSystemTitle: Why the system font is first.
designFonts.helpSystem: It is the fastest possible answer: nothing to download, nothing to wait for, no third party involved. For most projects it is also the right one — a custom font earns its cost only when the brand actually depends on it.

designType.intro: One number changes the whole set: headings, body text, captions — all of it, proportions intact.
designType.scaleHint: A multiplier over the project scale. 1.0 is the size the project ships with.
designType.leadingHint: The space between lines of body text. Lower is denser, higher is airier.
designType.previewBody: And this is body text underneath it — the size most of your visitors will actually read.
designType.helpLabel: Why one multiplier and not nine separate sizes
designType.helpWhyTitle: Nine fields are nine ways to break the scale.
designType.helpWhy: A subtitle larger than its heading, body text smaller than a caption — that is exactly the disarray this project spent a day removing from its code. A multiplier moves everything at once and keeps the proportions: the set is either bigger or smaller, never inconsistent.
designType.helpRange: Between 0.75 and 1.5. Outside it text is either unreadable or breaks the layout, and you would only discover that by opening every page. The limit lives in the application, not in this form — a value has to be checked where it arrives, not where it is typed.
designType.helpLive: The value is written into DESIGN-CONFIG on your server; the application reads it on every render as a CSS variable, and each step of the scale is calculated from it. The change shows on the next page load.

designShape.intro: Corners, borders and breathing room — the shape of every surface on the site.
designShape.radiusHint: Applies to cards, panels, buttons and inputs at once — each derives its own radius from this one value.
designShape.borderHint: A two-pixel border changes the character of an interface more than a colour does.
designShape.spaceHint: Vertical breathing room on every page. Content pages and work screens keep their difference — this moves both together.
designShape.widthHint: How wide the middle column of a page may grow. The header, the first screen and the footer are always full width.
designShape.previewBody: Its text sits inside the border, at the distance the density sets.
designShape.helpLabel: How these four values reach the pages
designShape.helpRadius: The project computes small, medium, large and extra-large corners from this single number, so a card, a button and an input never disagree. Setting them separately is how interfaces end up with three different corners on one screen.
designShape.helpSpaceTitle: Density is a multiplier, not a number of pixels.
designShape.helpSpace: Content pages are airier than work screens on purpose: one is read, the other is worked in. The multiplier moves both and keeps that difference — separate fields would let a work screen become airier than a content page, which is not a setting but a defect.
designShape.helpWidth: The page header, the first screen, the closing section and the footer are always full width. This value limits the column between them — the one the reader's eye travels along, where an over-long line becomes hard to follow.

designColors.intro: Seven roles, two themes. Each colour is an override: leave it untouched and the project theme decides.

primary.label: Brand colour
primary.description: Buttons, links, active states. The one colour a visitor will remember.

accent.label: Accent
accent.description: Highlights and hovers — a quieter relative of the brand colour.

muted.label: Muted surface
muted.description: Cards, panels, the background of secondary blocks.

border.label: Borders
border.description: Lines between elements — the quietest colour on the page.

designColors.contrastHint: Text against the page background. Below 4.5 the text fails the accessibility threshold for normal sizes.
designColors.previewBody: And the body text under it, in the colour people will actually read.
designColors.helpLabel: How colours reach the site, and what is computed for you
designColors.helpPairTitle: The text on a button is computed, not asked for.
designColors.helpPair: Every coloured role has a paired text colour on top of it. Change the brand colour and leave the pair alone, and a light brand colour keeps white text — a button whose label cannot be seen. The application derives that pair from the brightness of your colour, so the label stays readable whatever you pick.
designColors.helpThemesTitle: Light and dark are separate values.
designColors.helpThemes: A colour set once is almost always wrong on the other theme: dark text on a dark background disappears entirely. Set only the theme you care about — the other keeps the project's.
designColors.helpContrastTitle: The contrast figure is a measurement, not an opinion.
designColors.helpContrast: It is the ratio between text and background as the accessibility standard defines it. 4.5 is the threshold for normal text, 3.0 for large. Below that the page is not 'a matter of taste' — part of your visitors cannot read it.
designColors.schemesHint: One press sets all seven roles in both themes. Adjust anything afterwards — the change stays; press the same scheme again and its values come back.
designColors.schemeCustom: Your own combination — no ready-made scheme matches it exactly.

mapDesign.intro: Four decisions in the order they matter: the fonts first, then how big the text is, then the shape of surfaces, then colour. Each applies to the whole site at once.
mapDesign.allDefault: Nothing has been changed yet — the site looks the way the project theme decided, and that is a legitimate state, not an unfinished one.
mapDesign.liveNote: Every value on this page is read from the same file the site applies, so what you see here is what visitors see. Changes take effect on the next page load, without a rebuild.

fonts.title: Fonts — the voice of the product, and the first cost of loading
body: Three roles, not one font: headings, body text and monospace solve different problems, and folding them into a single field robs a product of its voice. The set opens on the system option, which takes the font already on the device — text is visible in the first frame and nothing leaves the page.

A catalogue instead of a text field removes three silent failures: a typo quietly falls back to the system font, a font without Cyrillic turns Russian text into rectangles, a forgotten URL leaves the name without the file. The build warns about none of them.

type.title: Typography — one multiplier instead of nine ways to break the scale
body: Text size is one number for the whole set: headings, body and captions move together and keep their proportions. Nine separate fields would look more generous and would let a subtitle grow larger than its heading.
This is not hypothetical: that exact disarray already existed here — nine different descriptions of a first-level heading — and removing it took a working day.

shape.title: Shapes and spacing — what reads as considered, or as rushed
body: One radius produces five: small, medium, large and extra-large are derived from it, so a card, a button and an input cannot disagree. Screens end up with three different corners exactly where each element decides for itself.

Density is a multiplier, not a pixel count: content pages are airier than work screens on purpose, and the multiplier moves both while keeping the difference. Width governs the middle of the page only — header, first screen and footer are always full width.

colors.title: Colours — ten ready schemes and a guard against the unreadable
body: A scheme sets all seven roles at once and in both themes: the visitor switches themes, so a decision describing only the light half would leave the dark one from the previous choice. Everything stays editable afterwards — your change lives on top of the scheme.

The label colour on a button is computed from the brightness of your colour, not asked for: otherwise a light brand colour would keep white text and produce a button whose label cannot be seen. Contrast is shown as a number while you choose — a measurement from the accessibility standard, not an opinion.

sections.title: Sections — reusable blocks of design
body: A page is assembled from sections — ready block kinds. A page material is data, not markup: the text lives separately and how it looks is the section decision. So a rule added to one kind reaches every page where that kind appears.
From this follows the point: the look of a project consists of exactly two things — the set of sections and the token values from the neighbouring pages. That is what makes a design portable.

The catalogue is open: eleven types by purpose, each with its kinds and a preview. Five of the ten landing types are covered today — the rest are shown empty, and that is a map of what is left to build, not a gap in the panel.
sections.hint: What pages are assembled from, and how a ready design is reused.

docs.shapeTitle: Shapes and spacing: what is already built
docs.sections: The rule, and what is coming
docs.sectionsTitle: Sections: how design is built and reused

developmentMode.lead: The mode decides one thing: whether a confirmed use case and an open step are required before work begins. Everything else — the technical laws of the project — holds in all four.
developmentMode.unavailable: Cannot read the settings file on the server. This is a deployment problem, not a wording one.
developmentMode.classicBody: Ordinary work by request: you say what to change, the agent changes it. No case, no step, no queue.
developmentMode.classicWhen: Take it for small, separate tasks — a fix, a wording, one page.
developmentMode.stepsBody: The agent breaks the task into numbered steps with sub-steps, and works the queue. What is planned survives the end of a session, because it is written down before it is executed.
developmentMode.stepsWhen: Take it when the work is longer than one conversation.
developmentMode.casesBody: The fullest order: the owner confirms use cases, they become products, products become a queue of steps. Nothing is built on a guess, and every step names the case it serves.
developmentMode.casesWhen: Take it when a product is being built, not patched.
developmentMode.migrationBody: Your project already exists. The agent reads its code — architecture, dependencies, what rests on what — lays out what it found as a file tree, and turns that tree into a queue of numbered steps. The frame comes first: addresses, tables, sign-in. Your data moves last, on access you grant yourself.
developmentMode.migrationWhen: Take it when the project is already written and needs moving, not starting over.
developmentMode.casesOpenHint: Save this mode and the Products group appears in the menu.
developmentMode.law: Static public pages, size limits, translations instead of inline text, settings read from config — these hold in every mode. A law that a mode could switch off would not be a law.
developmentMode.helpWhere: In PLATFORM-CONFIG on the server, beside the feature switches. The agent reads it at the start of a session, so it survives the end of a conversation — which is why this is a setting and not a phrase said in chat.
developmentMode.helpCost: Use cases cost more than steps, and steps more than classic — in tokens and in your time. That is the trade-off, and it is yours to make. The model is a requirement, not a ban: the badges on the cards name the model each mode was built for, and nothing here stops you from choosing otherwise. Use cases and a migration are the heavy ones: they hold a long chain of reasoning across a whole session, and a twenty-dollar plan usually runs out of room mid-way. A Max plan is what they were built for.
developmentMode.migrationOpenHint: Save this mode and the "Move to Fractera" tab appears — that is where you give the address of your repository or point at the folder on your machine.

intake.label: Intake
intake.hint: Questions, answers, Quiz, and the owner confirming the cases.

decomposition.label: Decomposition
decomposition.hint: Confirmed cases become an ordered queue of development steps.

development.label: Development
development.hint: The steps are worked one after another.

analysis.label: Analysis
analysis.hint: The result is studied; from it come new steps or a new decomposition.

productPage.sectionIntakeHint: What was asked and what you answered. The Quiz works from these answers, and everything after them stands on this.
productPage.intakeClosed: The intake is finished and does not reopen. To describe the product from scratch use Start over — it archives everything first.
productPage.intakeEmpty: No questions yet. They appear once the product structure is chosen.
productPage.sectionQuizHint: The whole dialogue with the model, kept as raw material. The cases are what came out of it.
